model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a festival in my town. It is a river festival and it happens every year in September, at the end of the summer.

So last year I took part in it. Normally I just go and watch, but last year my aunt has a food stall, so I helped her. We started very early in the morning, and we made pancakes, I think maybe two hundred, it was a lot. The stall was next to the river, so we can see everything.

In the evening people put lanterns on the water. There is music, and everybody walks along the river together. I also meet my old school friend there, we didn't see each other for a long time, so that was nice.

I enjoyed it very much because it was different. When you work in the festival you see many things that other people don't see. Also I was very tired but happy. The town is usually quiet, but on this day it is not quiet, everybody is outside. So it was a very good day and this is the festival I took part in.

what_caps_it.point: The past tense breaks into the present four times inside one short story.
'Nice', 'good', 'a lot', 'different' — the whole evaluation runs on flat words.
Almost every link is 'so' or 'also', and the close restates the card.

annotations.span: we made pancakes, I think maybe two hundred
annotations.label: Gives a number, not 'a lot'
annotations.why: Keep this — one number makes an examiner believe the whole story.

annotations.span: my aunt has a food stall
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'my aunt had a food stall' and stay back there for the rest.

annotations.span: so we can see everything
annotations.label: Modal slips out of the past
annotations.why: 'We could see everything' — past modals matter as much as past verbs.

annotations.span: I also meet my old school friend there, we didn't see each other for a long time
annotations.label: Two tenses missing at once
annotations.why: 'I bumped into a friend I hadn't seen for years' fixes both in one clause.

annotations.span: So it was a very good day and this is the festival I took part in.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: Land on a thought about the day instead of a summary of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same day, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the river festival in my home town, which happens every year at the end of the summer — and specifically about last September, because that was the first year I actually took part in it rather than just turning up to watch.

My aunt runs a food stall there, and she'd asked me back in August whether I'd give her a hand, so I said yes without really thinking about what that would involve. What it involved was a six o'clock start. She'd already been up mixing batter by the time I arrived, and by lunchtime we'd turned out something like two hundred pancakes between us. I'd more or less stopped being able to feel my arms.

The stall was right on the riverbank, though, which meant we had easily the best view in town. At dusk everybody brings paper lanterns down to the water and floats them out, and there's a procession along both banks with a brass band at the front. By about eight the whole thing was in full swing. I also bumped into a friend I hadn't seen since school, which I wasn't expecting at all.

What I enjoyed most, though, wasn't the lanterns — it was being on the inside of it. When you're behind a stall you notice things you'd never notice as a visitor: who knows everybody, which families have been doing the same thing for years, and how much work sits underneath three hours that are supposed to look effortless. I'd watched that festival my whole life, and I'd never once thought about who was putting it on.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects put the preparation behind the day instead of beside it.
'Give her a hand', 'in full swing', 'bumped into' replace 'nice' and 'good'.
A cleft announces the fourth bullet, so the evaluation cannot be skipped.

annotations.span: because that was the first year I actually took part in it rather than just turning up to watch
annotations.label: Narrows to one year
annotations.why: Say what makes this instance different in sentence one and the story writes itself.

annotations.span: she'd asked me back in August whether I'd give her a hand
annotations.label: Past perfect plus reported question
annotations.why: Reported questions keep statement order — 'whether I'd', never 'whether would I'.

annotations.span: She'd already been up mixing batter by the time I arrived
annotations.label: Two layers of past time
annotations.why: Use one 'by the time' sentence per story to show sequencing.

annotations.span: in full swing
annotations.label: Idiom used where it belongs
annotations.why: Reuse it for any event at its busiest — a market, a party, a match.

annotations.span: bumped into a friend I hadn't seen since school
annotations.label: Phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Bumped into' says by chance in two words; 'met accidentally' does not.

annotations.span: What I enjoyed most, though, wasn't the lanterns — it was being on the inside of it.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the last bullet

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The one I want to talk about is a river festival my home town has been putting on for as long as anyone can remember, always at the tail end of the summer. Last September was the first year I was on the working side of it rather than the wandering-around side.

My aunt has had a food stall there for the best part of a decade, and she'd asked me in August whether I'd help out, which I'd agreed to before I'd properly thought it through. Thinking it through would have meant noticing the six o'clock start. She was already mixing batter by the time I turned up, and by the middle of the day we'd produced somewhere in the region of two hundred pancakes and I had no feeling left in my forearms.

What the stall did give us was the riverbank, which is where the whole thing actually happens. At dusk people float paper lanterns out onto the water and a procession works its way along both banks behind a fairly ragged brass band.

Not that the lanterns were the part that stayed with me. What stayed with me was the view from behind the stall, because from there you see the machinery. You see which families have been running the same three metres of pavement for thirty years, and how much unglamorous work sits underneath something that is meant to look spontaneous. I'd watched that festival every year of my life without once wondering who was making it happen.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous and a stacked past perfect where band 7 used one layer.
'The tail end', 'in the region of', 'the machinery' — idiom placed, not displayed.
The close names what the story is an example of instead of summarising it.

annotations.span: has been putting on for as long as anyone can remember
annotations.label: Perfect continuous for duration
annotations.why: Use it once for anything still going on now that started long ago.

annotations.span: which I'd agreed to before I'd properly thought it through
annotations.label: Two past perfects in one clause
annotations.why: Stack them only where the order genuinely matters, as it does here.

annotations.span: at the tail end of the summer
annotations.label: Idiom sitting naturally
annotations.why: Two well-placed idioms beat five decorative ones every single time.

annotations.span: from there you see the machinery
annotations.label: One metaphor carries the point
annotations.why: 'The machinery' says hidden organised effort without a single extra clause.

annotations.span: I'd watched that festival every year of my life without once wondering who was making it happen.
annotations.label: Close lifts out of the anecdote
annotations.why: End on what the story is an example of, not on what happened.

model_answers.label: A typical band 6 answer
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to describe a song which reminds me of one place. It is an old song with guitar. I don't know the name of the band exactly, but my brother is playing it all the time.

The place is a campsite near the sea. When I was nineteen I work there for the summer, in the kitchen. My brother has a van and he drives me there every morning, and this song is always on. So now when I hear it I remember this road and I remember the sea.

The summer was very hard because we work many hours and the money was not good. But it was also very nice, because we were young and we have no responsibility.

Two years ago I heard this song in a supermarket. It was very strange, because for one moment I am not in the supermarket, I am in the van again. I think music can do this and other things cannot do this. So this is the song, and this is the reason it is special for me.

what_caps_it.point: The past narrative slides into the present in five separate places.
'Very hard', 'not good', 'very nice', 'very strange' — adjectives with 'very' in front.
Two sentences repeat almost word for word, and the close restates the card.

annotations.span: for one moment I am not in the supermarket, I am in the van again
annotations.label: Shows the effect, doesn't state it
annotations.why: Keep this — showing the moment is worth more than saying 'it was emotional'.

annotations.span: my brother is playing it all the time
annotations.label: Present continuous for a past habit
annotations.why: Use 'he'd play it constantly' — 'would' is the natural form for repeated past.

annotations.span: I work there for the summer
annotations.label: Bare present inside a past clause
annotations.why: 'When I was nineteen I worked there' — both halves must agree.

annotations.span: we have no responsibility
annotations.label: Tense slips again at the end
annotations.why: 'We had nothing to worry about' keeps the tense and improves the phrase.

annotations.span: So this is the song, and this is the reason it is special for me.
annotations.label: Ending recycles the prompt
annotations.why: Finish on an idea about music, not on a restatement of the task.

model_answers.label: Same summer, band 7 language
model_answers.transcript:
The piece of music I'd pick is a fairly slow guitar track that my older brother used to play constantly. I couldn't tell you the name of the band even now, which probably says something about how I came across it in the first place.

It's tied to one specific place: a campsite on the coast about two hours from where we grew up. The summer I turned nineteen I worked there in the kitchen, and my brother had a van and a job on the same site, so he'd drive us both over at seven every morning with that album on. By the end of August I must have heard it a couple of hundred times, and I'd honestly stopped noticing it at all.

It was a hard summer — long shifts, terrible pay, and the two of us sharing a tent that leaked whenever it rained. But it's also the last summer I can remember having absolutely nothing to worry about, and the song seems to have absorbed all of that. I wouldn't have chosen it as a soundtrack for any of it, but you don't really get to choose.

What gets me is what happened a couple of years ago. I was standing in a supermarket and it came on over the speakers, and for about three seconds I wasn't in the supermarket at all — I was in the passenger seat with the window down. A photograph shows you the place, whereas a song puts you back inside it, and I've never really worked out how that happens.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Would' for repeated past and a modal perfect replace the flat present-tense run.
'Tied to', 'absorbed', 'came on over the speakers' — verbs doing precise work.
A cleft and a 'whereas' contrast give the last forty seconds visible shape.

annotations.span: It's tied to one specific place
annotations.label: Narrows before describing
annotations.why: Announce the link early so the examiner knows where the answer is going.

annotations.span: he'd drive us both over at seven every morning
annotations.label: 'Would' for a repeated past action
annotations.why: Any routine in a past story can take 'd rather than a plain past.

annotations.span: I must have heard it a couple of hundred times
annotations.label: Modal perfect for an estimate
annotations.why: 'Must have' turns a guess into a structure worth grammar credit.

annotations.span: long shifts, terrible pay, and the two of us sharing a tent that leaked
annotations.label: Three details, no verbs wasted
annotations.why: A quick list of three buys ten seconds and sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: the song seems to have absorbed all of that
annotations.label: One verb replaces a sentence
annotations.why: 'Absorbed' does the work of 'it makes me remember all these feelings'.

annotations.span: What gets me is what happened a couple of years ago.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Saying 'what gets me is' commits you to explaining, not describing.

annotations.span: I was in the passenger seat with the window down
annotations.label: Slow down on the image
annotations.why: Drop the pace on the picture so the listener sees it too.

annotations.span: A photograph shows you the place, whereas a song puts you back inside it
annotations.label: Contrast built from two verbs
annotations.why: 'Shows' against 'puts you inside' is sharper than any adjective pair.

model_answers.label: One step further up
model_answers.transcript:
The track I'd go for is a slow, fairly unremarkable guitar piece that my older brother wore out one particular summer. I still couldn't name the band, which tells you that I didn't so much choose this music as get handed it.

What it's welded to is a campsite on the coast, two hours or so from where we grew up. The summer I turned nineteen I was working in the kitchen there, my brother had a van and a job on the same site, and he'd drive us over at seven with that album going. Not once, in three months, did he put anything else on. By September I'd stopped hearing it altogether.

It wasn't a good summer by any sensible measure — the shifts were brutal, the pay was worse, and our tent leaked whenever it rained hard enough to matter. It was, though, the last stretch of my life with nothing hanging over it, and somehow the record has taken all of that on board.

The strange part came years later. I'd have said, if anyone had asked, that I felt nothing whatsoever about that album. Then it started up over the speakers in a supermarket, and for three or four seconds the supermarket simply wasn't there. A photograph hands you a place from the outside; a song drops you back into the middle of it, which is why I think music does something to memory that nothing else quite manages.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion after 'not once' where band 7 used ordinary word order.
'Wore out', 'welded to', 'taken all of that on board' — idiom placed, not paraded.
The close states a general claim about memory rather than the speaker's feeling.

annotations.span: Not once, in three months, did he put anything else on.
annotations.label: Negative inversion
annotations.why: Front a negative adverbial and invert — a single sentence lifts the register.

annotations.span: I didn't so much choose this music as get handed it
annotations.label: 'Not so much... as' structure
annotations.why: Use it whenever you want to correct one description with a better one.

annotations.span: What it's welded to is a campsite on the coast
annotations.label: A stronger verb than 'connected'
annotations.why: 'Welded' says permanent and involuntary in one word.

annotations.span: the record has taken all of that on board
annotations.label: Everyday idiom, exact fit
annotations.why: Common phrasing used precisely outscores rare words used loosely.

annotations.span: which is why I think music does something to memory that nothing else quite manages
annotations.label: Generalises on the way out
annotations.why: Close on the claim your story supports, then stop talking.

model_answers.label: Clear enough, capped by grammar
model_answers.transcript:
I want to recommend a book. It is a small book, maybe two hundred pages, and a colleague gave it to me two years ago.

The story was about a man who left his village when he was young. After thirty years he came back and nobody remembered him. He met his sister and she was very angry with him. That is the main story, there is not so much action. It was quite sad but also it was funny sometimes.

I read it on the train. I was going to my parents, it is five hours, so I finished it in one day. Normally I read very slow, so this was unusual for me.

I recommend it to people of my age because it is short. Many people say they have no time for reading, but this book you can read in one day. Also the writer doesn't explain everything. He gives you the situation and you must think yourself. I like this very much. So this is a very good book and I recommend it to everybody.

what_caps_it.point: The plot is told in the past, which is the standard error on any media card.
'Sad', 'funny', 'good', 'unusual' — four flat adjectives carry the whole judgement.
The close simply repeats the opening sentence with 'very' added.

annotations.span: Many people say they have no time for reading, but this book you can read in one day.
annotations.label: Answers the objection first
annotations.why: Keep this — meeting the obvious counter-argument makes a recommendation land.

annotations.span: The story was about a man who left his village when he was young.
annotations.label: Plot told in the past tense
annotations.why: Say 'it follows a man who leaves his village' — plot is always present simple.

annotations.span: It was quite sad but also it was funny sometimes.
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives, no evidence
annotations.why: Name one scene instead; 'sad' proves nothing on its own.

annotations.span: Normally I read very slow
annotations.label: Adjective used as an adverb
annotations.why: 'I read slowly' — or better, 'I'm a slow reader'.

annotations.span: So this is a very good book and I recommend it to everybody.
annotations.label: Ending restates the opening
annotations.why: Land on a claim about reading, not a repeat of the task.

model_answers.label: The same book at band 7
model_answers.transcript:
The book I'd recommend is a short novel — barely two hundred pages — that a colleague pushed on me a couple of years ago, more or less insisting I take it home that evening.

It follows a man who leaves his village at eighteen and comes back thirty years later expecting to be recognised. He isn't. His sister is still living there, and she's furious with him in a way he hasn't prepared for at all. That's really the whole plot; there isn't a great deal of incident in it. What there is instead is a lot of quiet, very exact conversation, and a village that has carried on perfectly well without him.

I read the whole thing in a day, on a train, going up to see my parents — five hours each way and nothing else to do. That almost never happens to me. There was no signal on the train, which probably helped more than the book did. I'm normally a slow reader who gives up around page forty.

The reason I'd press it on anyone my age is partly that it's short, which sounds like a weak recommendation until you consider how many people say flatly that they haven't got time to read. The real reason, though, is that it refuses to explain itself. The author sets a scene, gives you two people talking, and leaves. You end up doing about half the work yourself, and I remembered it far better than books that had spelled everything out for me.

what_lifts_it.point: Plot in the present simple, reading in the past, and one past perfect at the close.
'Pushed on me', 'refuses to explain itself', 'spelled everything out' — verbs, not adjectives.
The recommendation is split into a weak reason and a real one, out loud.

annotations.span: leaves his village at eighteen and comes back thirty years later expecting to be recognised
annotations.label: Present simple for plot
annotations.why: Every plot verb stays present, however long ago you read it.

annotations.span: she's furious with him in a way he hasn't prepared for at all
annotations.label: Present perfect inside a plot summary
annotations.why: It shows the character's history without leaving the present frame.

annotations.span: a colleague pushed on me
annotations.label: One verb replaces three
annotations.why: 'Pushed on me' carries insistence that 'gave me' throws away.

annotations.span: That's really the whole plot; there isn't a great deal of incident in it.
annotations.label: Stops the plot early
annotations.why: Say the plot is finished and you free thirty seconds for judgement.

annotations.span: The reason I'd press it on anyone my age is partly that it's short
annotations.label: Signposts the last bullet
annotations.why: 'Partly' promises a second reason, which keeps the listener with you.

annotations.span: it refuses to explain itself
annotations.label: Personification doing real work
annotations.why: Give the book the verb and you sound like a reader, not a summariser.

annotations.span: You end up doing about half the work yourself
annotations.label: Evaluates instead of describing
annotations.why: Say what the book asks of a reader, not what it contains.

annotations.span: The author sets a scene, gives you two people talking, and leaves.
annotations.label: Three beats, falling on 'leaves'
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop hard on the last word so the sentence lands.

model_answers.label: The next step up
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd hand to someone my age is a short novel, two hundred pages at most, that a colleague more or less forced on me a couple of years back. She wouldn't take no for an answer, which turned out to be sound judgement on her part.

It follows a man who walks out of his village at eighteen and returns three decades later half expecting a welcome. What he gets is indifference. His sister is still in the same house and is angrier than he has any framework for understanding. Very little else happens. What the book consists of is conversation — quiet, exact, and full of things nobody is prepared to say directly.

I read it in a single day on a train, which I can't remember doing before or since. Left to myself I stall somewhere around page forty and never go back. There was no signal on that train either, which I suspect did as much work as the writing.

Why recommend it to people our age in particular. Partly the length, which sounds like faint praise until you count how many of us claim to have no time. Mainly, though, because it declines to explain itself. Scenes are set, people speak, the author withdraws, and the reader is left holding roughly half the meaning. What stayed with me was not the story so much as the discovery that being trusted to work something out is far more memorable than being told it.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive run and 'not so much... as' where band 7 used plain active clauses.
'Wouldn't take no for an answer', 'faint praise', 'declines to' — precise, unshowy choices.
The close turns the recommendation into a general claim about how people learn.

annotations.span: Scenes are set, people speak, the author withdraws
annotations.label: Passive in a three-part run
annotations.why: The passive keeps the reader's attention on the book, not the writer.

annotations.span: not the story so much as the discovery
annotations.label: 'Not so much as' comparison
annotations.why: Use it to correct your own first description with a sharper one.

annotations.span: She wouldn't take no for an answer
annotations.label: Idiom exactly where it fits
annotations.why: Everyday idiom placed well beats a rare word placed badly.

annotations.span: which sounds like faint praise
annotations.label: A precise, unshowy phrase
annotations.why: 'Faint praise' names a whole attitude in two words.

annotations.span: being trusted to work something out is far more memorable than being told it
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Close by naming the principle your example demonstrates.

model_answers.transcript:
I will describe a dish which I learned to cook. It is a stew with lentils and tomato. It is very simple, only one pan.

I learned it from my flatmate mother. She lives in another country, and when my flatmate calls her, one time I ask her about this food, and she explain me how to make it on the phone. I write it on a paper.

Now I make it maybe one time in a week. First you cut the onion, then you put the tomato, and after you put the lentils and water, and then you wait forty minutes. It is very cheap also, and this is important because I am student.

The reason I want to learn this dish is my first winter here I have no money and I eat very bad. My flatmate cooks this one evening and he gives me some, and it was the first time I feel okay in that flat. So for me it is not only food. So this is the dish that I learned to cook.

what_caps_it.point: Third-person -s, the possessive -s and the past tense all disappear in turn.
Three sentences begin with 'so', and the close repeats the opening line.
'Very simple', 'very cheap', 'very bad' — an adjective with 'very' in front of it.

annotations.span: First you cut the onion, then you put the tomato, and after you put the lentils and water
annotations.label: Process kept in order
annotations.why: Keep this — sequencing words are cheap and they make you sound organised.

annotations.span: I learned it from my flatmate mother.
annotations.label: Possessive -s missing
annotations.why: 'My flatmate's mother' — the apostrophe s is what links the two people.

annotations.span: she explain me how to make it on the phone
annotations.label: Third-person -s and a preposition
annotations.why: 'She explained it to me' — explain always needs 'to' before the person.

annotations.span: my first winter here I have no money and I eat very bad
annotations.label: Past narrative told in the present
annotations.why: 'I had no money and I ate badly' — one anchor, then hold the past.

annotations.span: So this is the dish that I learned to cook.
annotations.label: Closes by quoting the card
annotations.why: End on what cooking it changed, not on the task wording.

model_answers.label: Band 7: identical dish, sharper words
model_answers.transcript:
The dish I'd talk about is a lentil and tomato stew — nothing sophisticated, one pan, about forty minutes from start to finish.

I got it from my flatmate's mother, of all people. She lives abroad, and he used to ring her every Sunday, and one week I asked whether she'd talk me through it. So she did, over a video call, while I stood in the kitchen with a notebook. She kept saying that the amounts didn't really matter, which I found quite hard to accept at the time.

I make it about once a week now, usually on a Sunday, so that there's something in the fridge on Monday. You soften an onion, in goes the tomato, then the lentils and a lot of water, and after that you more or less leave it alone. The only thing that matters is not rushing the onion, and that took me roughly six attempts to learn. Everything else about it is forgiving, which is the only reason I still make it.

As for why that particular dish — my first winter here I was living on toast and whatever had been reduced, and I felt fairly grim about the whole thing. My flatmate made this one evening and handed me a bowl, and it was the first thing I'd eaten in that flat that tasted like somebody had bothered. So learning it wasn't really about the recipe. It was about not wanting to go back to living the way I had been.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Used to', a past perfect and a purpose clause replace a run of flat present verbs.
'Talk me through it', 'living on toast', 'somebody had bothered' — chunks, not adjectives.
'As for why' announces the fourth bullet, so the reason cannot get lost.

annotations.span: nothing sophisticated, one pan, about forty minutes from start to finish
annotations.label: Orients in one breath
annotations.why: Three facts in the first sentence buy you the listener's patience.

annotations.span: he used to ring her every Sunday
annotations.label: 'Used to' for a past routine
annotations.why: Any repeated past habit is worth one 'used to' rather than a plain past.

annotations.span: talk me through it
annotations.label: Phrasal verb, exactly right
annotations.why: 'Talk through' means explain step by step — reuse it for any process.

annotations.span: You soften an onion, in goes the tomato, then the lentils and a lot of water
annotations.label: Process, no wasted verbs
annotations.why: 'In goes the tomato' inverts for pace and keeps the recipe moving.

annotations.span: As for why that particular dish
annotations.label: Names the last bullet aloud
annotations.why: Say the move and you will not forget to make it.

annotations.span: living on toast and whatever had been reduced
annotations.label: Two chunks doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Living on' plus 'reduced' says poor without ever saying poor.

annotations.span: it was the first thing I'd eaten in that flat that tasted like somebody had bothered
annotations.label: Past perfect twice, correctly
annotations.why: Use it when one past event sits inside another; here it does.

annotations.span: It was about not wanting to go back to living the way I had been.
annotations.label: Falls on 'had been'
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop across the final clause so the turn sounds closed.

model_answers.label: Band 8: sustained, not flashy
model_answers.transcript:
The dish is a lentil and tomato stew, which is about as unsophisticated as cooking gets — one pan, four ingredients, three quarters of an hour — and I make more of it than of anything else I know how to make.

It reached me second-hand, from my flatmate's mother, who lives on the other side of the world and whom I have still never met. He rang her every Sunday without fail, and one week I asked whether she'd take me through it. She did, over a video call, while I stood in the kitchen writing down things she plainly thought did not need writing down. Her only real instruction was that the quantities were beside the point, which struck me then as unhelpful and strikes me now as the entire lesson.

These days it's a Sunday job, so that Monday looks after itself. You soften the onion properly — that is the whole trick, and it took me half a dozen goes to stop hurrying it — and everything afterwards is a matter of waiting for it to thicken.

Why this one, though. My first winter here I was living on toast and whatever the supermarket had marked down, and I was fairly miserable without ever quite admitting it. He handed me a bowl of this one evening, and it was the first food in that flat that tasted as though somebody had made an effort. What I actually learned that day had very little to do with lentils.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Whom' in a relative clause and a then-and-now tense pairing in one sentence.
'Beside the point', 'marked down', 'looks after itself' — idiom placed, not paraded.
The close withholds the lesson instead of announcing it, which makes it land.

annotations.span: whom I have still never met
annotations.label: Object relative with 'whom'
annotations.why: One 'whom' per turn is enough; more sounds studied rather than fluent.

annotations.span: which struck me then as unhelpful and strikes me now as the entire lesson
annotations.label: Past and present in one clause
annotations.why: Pair the two tenses to show that your view of something changed.

annotations.span: the quantities were beside the point
annotations.label: Idiom in exactly the right slot

cue_card.topic: Describe a place to eat that you would take a visitor to.
bullets: where the place is
what sort of food it serves
who you would take there
and explain why you would choose it rather than somewhere better known.

teaching.band_move: Replace every second 'there is' with a relative clause. Flat listing is what caps place cards at six.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take the place you have eaten in most recently, not the grandest one you know. You need the layout in your head, not the reputation.

note_grid.cell: under rail bridge, 5 min fr station
1 dish/day on board, fish or beans
famous places now priced for tourists

prep_plan.trap: Candidates describe the food and never once say where the place actually is.

time_plan.goal: Place it on a map in one sentence.
The building, then what comes out of the kitchen.
One visitor, and how they reacted.
Why this over the obvious choice.
One line about showing a city honestly.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe the doorway, the board outside and what is written on it.

error_watchlist.wrong: The café is in the bridge, near to the station.
error_watchlist.right: The café is under the bridge, near the station.
error_watchlist.why: 'Near' takes no 'to', and 'under' is not 'in'.

error_watchlist.pattern: word order with objects and adverbs
error_watchlist.wrong: I took there my cousin last spring.
error_watchlist.right: I took my cousin there last spring.
error_watchlist.why: Object first, then place, then time.

error_watchlist.wrong: In this café you see normal people of the neighbourhood.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Describing a place produces long noun phrases, and a pause inside one destroys the picture.

target_words.note: One unit; never pause before it.
Compound noun — stress the first half.
Another compound, stressed at the front.
Two beats in speech, not three.

chunking_drill.sentence: There's no sign, just a doorway and a blackboard propped against the wall

teaching.examiner_note: You will not be asked to justify your choice during the long turn. Save the justification for the fourth bullet, where it earns marks.

swap_slots.span: a railway bridge about five minutes from the main station
swap_slots.prompt: Your own location, with one distance and one landmark. Never simply 'in the centre'.

swap_slots.span: six tables
swap_slots.prompt: Your own scale, as a number. Size is the fastest way to make a room real.

swap_slots.span: a bean soup that I'd happily eat every week for the rest of my life
swap_slots.prompt: Your own dish plus the exaggeration you'd actually use about it out loud.

swap_slots.span: my cousin there last spring
swap_slots.prompt: Your own visitor and when. One relationship, one season, nothing more.

teaching.transfer_drill: Describe the place you'd take the same visitor for a walk, using position phrases rather than adjectives. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: The common plateau answer
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a small café where I take my friends when they come to visit. It is under the railway bridge, near the station, in the old part of the city.

There is not a sign outside. There are six tables and there is a board with the food of the day. Two brothers are working there, they cook and also they serve. Every day there is only one dish, so you cannot choose. Sometimes it is fish, sometimes it is a soup with beans.

I take there my cousin last year. She lives in another city and she wanted to see something typical. She was surprised because the place is very small and it is not beautiful, but the food was very good and it was very cheap also.

I choose this place because the famous restaurants in my city are for the tourists. They are expensive and the food is not real. But in this café you see the normal people of the neighbourhood. So this is the place where I take the visitors.

what_caps_it.point: Five sentences begin 'there is' or 'there are'; the room is listed, not described.
'I take there my cousin' puts the object after the place, and the tense is wrong.
'Very small', 'very good', 'very cheap' — the same intensifier three times.

annotations.span: Every day there is only one dish, so you cannot choose.
annotations.label: One fact that defines the place
annotations.why: Keep this — a single distinguishing detail is worth ten adjectives.

annotations.span: There are six tables and there is a board with the food of the day.
annotations.label: Flat existential listing
annotations.why: Join them: 'six tables and a board that tells you what you're eating'.

annotations.span: I take there my cousin last year.
annotations.label: Word order and tense both wrong
annotations.why: 'I took my cousin there last year' — object, then place, then time.

annotations.span: the food was very good and it was very cheap also
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives and a stray 'also'
annotations.why: Say what it cost, or what it tasted of. Evidence, not intensifiers.

annotations.span: So this is the place where I take the visitors.
annotations.label: Ending copies the prompt
annotations.why: Close on what showing that place says about your city.

model_answers.label: Band 7: same café, better tools
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd take somebody is a café tucked in underneath a railway bridge about five minutes from the main station — the sort of place you'd walk past twice before you found it.

There's no sign, just a doorway and a blackboard propped against the wall. Inside there are six tables, and it's run by two brothers who cook, serve and take the money between them. The blackboard is the whole menu: one dish a day, no choice at all. Some days that's fish, some days it's a bean soup that I'd happily eat every week for the rest of my life. You pay at the counter on the way out, and nobody has ever given me a bill.

I took my cousin there last spring, when she came up for a few days. She'd asked to see something typical, and I could tell from her face on the way in that she thought I'd misunderstood the request. She'd changed her mind by the time the plates arrived. She asked me to write the name down before she left.

The reason I'd choose it over somewhere better known is that the famous places in this city have quietly stopped being for the people who live here. They've been priced for visitors, and the food has been softened to match. In that café, though, you sit next to whoever happens to work on that street, and you eat what they eat. If somebody's only got two days, I'd rather they saw that than a photograph of it.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive, a relative clause and a past perfect replace the run of 'there is'.
'Tucked in underneath', 'propped against', 'softened to match' — position and judgement.
The last bullet is announced and then argued, rather than asserted once.

annotations.span: the sort of place you'd walk past twice before you found it
annotations.label: Judges while describing
annotations.why: One evaluative clause in the opening tells the examiner an opinion is coming.

annotations.span: tucked in underneath
annotations.label: Position phrase, not an adjective
annotations.why: Reuse it for anything half-hidden: a shop, a house, a path.

annotations.span: it's run by two brothers who cook, serve and take the money between them
annotations.label: Passive plus relative clause
annotations.why: This is the fix for flat listing — put the people inside the sentence.

annotations.span: The blackboard is the whole menu: one dish a day, no choice at all.
annotations.label: One detail carries the character
annotations.why: Choose the fact that could only be true of your place, and lead with it.

annotations.span: She'd changed her mind by the time the plates arrived.
annotations.label: Past perfect for the turn
annotations.why: 'By the time' plus past perfect is a whole story in one sentence.

annotations.span: The reason I'd choose it over somewhere better known is
annotations.label: Names the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Saying the move out loud stops you drifting back into description.

annotations.span: They've been priced for visitors, and the food has been softened to match.
annotations.label: 'Softened' does the criticism
annotations.why: One verb can carry a judgement that three adjectives would blur.

annotations.span: I'd rather they saw that than a photograph of it
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'that'
annotations.why: Contrastive stress makes the comparison audible without extra words.

model_answers.label: Band 8: sustained, not decorated
model_answers.transcript:
If somebody came to stay, I'd take them to a café wedged under a railway arch about five minutes' walk from the station — one of those places you could pass a dozen times without ever registering it.

There is no sign. There's a doorway, a blackboard leaning against the brickwork, and inside, six tables and two brothers who between them do the cooking, the serving and the till. The blackboard is the menu in its entirety: one dish, that day, take it or leave it. Occasionally fish; more often a bean soup I would cheerfully eat until I died. You settle up at the counter on the way out and no bill has ever appeared.

My cousin came up last spring and asked to see something typical, and I could tell as we went in that she suspected me of having misheard her. By the time the plates were down she had revised that view considerably, and she wrote the name down before she left.

What makes me choose it over the well-known places is that those have quietly stopped belonging to the people who live here. Prices have been set with visitors in mind and the cooking has been smoothed out to match, which is a shame but is hardly a mystery. In that café you eat beside whoever works on the street outside, and you eat what they eat. Given two days in a city, I'd sooner show someone that than a tidier version of it.

what_lifts_it.point: A second conditional opening and a double passive where band 7 used plain statements.
'Wedged', 'take it or leave it', 'smoothed out' — precision rather than display.
The close judges the alternative instead of restating the choice already made.

annotations.span: If somebody came to stay, I'd take them to a café
annotations.label: Second conditional opener
annotations.why: It answers a 'would' card in the tense the card is actually written in.

annotations.span: Prices have been set with visitors in mind and the cooking has been smoothed out to match
annotations.label: Two passives, one point
annotations.why: The passive hides the agent, which is exactly the criticism being made.

annotations.span: wedged under a railway arch
annotations.label: Verb chosen for its force
annotations.why: 'Wedged' says squeezed into a gap that was not designed for it.

annotations.span: take it or leave it
annotations.label: Four words, whole attitude
annotations.why: Plain everyday idiom used precisely reads as fluency, never as revision.

annotations.span: I'd sooner show someone that than a tidier version of it
annotations.label: Close lands on a judgement
annotations.why: End by comparing your choice with the alternative you rejected.

I want to talk about swimming, because I want to be better in swimming.

Now I am not very good. I can swim, but only maybe two hundred metres, and after that I must stop because I am very tired. My technique is not good. I learn to swim when I was a child in a lake, so nobody teach me the correct way.

For improving I think I need lessons. There is a coach in my pool and he gives lessons two times in a week. Also I must practise the breathing, because now I breathe only in one side and this is a problem for my speed.

Why it is important for me? Before, I am running every morning. Then two years ago I hurt my knee and the doctor said no more running. So now swimming is the only sport for me. annotations.why: 'Twice a week' — 'a week' is the standard form, never 'in a week'.

model_answers.label: Band 7: the same plan, argued
model_answers.transcript:
The activity I'd like to be better at is swimming, which is slightly embarrassing to have to admit at thirty-one.

I can swim, in the sense that I don't sink. What I can't do is swim well. Two hundred metres and I'm hanging off the end of the lane getting my breath back, mainly because my technique has never been corrected. I learned in a lake as a child, by watching my brother and copying him badly, and nobody has told me what I'm doing wrong since. I don't think it has occurred to anybody that it might need saying.

What I'd need to do is fairly obvious, which is the annoying part. There's a coach at my local pool who does technique sessions twice a week, and I'd have to actually go to those rather than telling myself I'll sort it out on my own. The other thing is breathing — I only breathe on one side, which means I swim slightly crooked, and I've been doing it that way for twenty years. Undoing that will be worse than learning it was.

As for why it matters, I used to run every morning, and then I did something fairly permanent to my knee a couple of years ago and had to stop. Swimming's the only thing left that empties my head in the same way. If I could get to a kilometre without stopping, I think I'd have got that back, and I've missed it a great deal more than I expected to.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive present perfect, a perfect continuous and a second conditional in one turn.
'Hanging off the end of the lane', 'empties my head' — concrete instead of abstract.
Each bullet is opened with a phrase that says which bullet is being answered.

annotations.span: I can swim, in the sense that I don't sink. What I can't do is swim well.
annotations.label: Grades the claim precisely
annotations.why: Qualify a claim and then correct it — that is what an honest self-assessment sounds like.

annotations.span: my technique has never been corrected
annotations.label: Passive present perfect
annotations.why: The passive puts the blame nowhere, which is exactly the meaning wanted.

annotations.span: hanging off the end of the lane getting my breath back
annotations.label: A picture, not an adjective
annotations.why: Describe what exhaustion looks like rather than saying you were tired.

annotations.span: What I'd need to do is fairly obvious, which is the annoying part.
annotations.label: Signposts and evaluates at once
annotations.why: Announcing the bullet and judging it buys you both structure and opinion.

annotations.span: I've been doing it that way for twenty years
annotations.label: Perfect continuous shows the span
annotations.why: Reach for it whenever a habit began long ago and is running still.

annotations.span: As for why it matters
annotations.label: Opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Three words that guarantee you answer the 'explain' line.

annotations.span: I did something fairly permanent to my knee
annotations.label: Understatement doing real work
annotations.why: Playing an injury down sounds far more natural than dramatising it.

annotations.span: I've missed it a great deal more than I expected to
annotations.label: Falls away on the last clause
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop through 'than I expected to' so the turn closes.

model_answers.label: Band 8: control, not decoration
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd like to be better at is swimming, which at thirty-one is not an easy thing to say out loud.

I can swim in the narrow sense that I do not sink. Swimming properly is another matter entirely. Two hundred metres in and I'm draped over the end of the lane getting my breath back, and the reason is simply that nobody has ever corrected a single thing I do. I taught myself in a lake at about eight, by watching my brother and copying him inaccurately, and that is still, twenty-three years later, the stroke I am using. Nobody has had cause to tell me otherwise, because nobody has ever watched.

What improvement would take is depressingly clear. There are technique sessions at the pool twice a week, and the only real obstacle is that I would have to attend them instead of telling myself I'll work it out alone. Then there's the breathing. I take air on one side only, which pulls me off line, and habits of that age do not go quietly. Twenty-three years is a long time to be leaning to the left.

As to why any of this matters — I ran every morning for years until I did something irreversible to a knee, and swimming is the one thing left that empties my head the same way. Were I to reach a kilometre unbroken, I suspect what I'd actually have recovered is the hour, rather than the distance.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion with 'were I to' where band 7 used a standard second conditional.
'Draped over', 'pulls me off line', 'do not go quietly' — vivid but unshowy.
The close distinguishes what he wants from what he says he wants.

annotations.span: Were I to reach a kilometre unbroken
annotations.label: Inversion for the conditional
annotations.why: Same meaning as 'if I reached', one register higher, still speakable.

annotations.span: habits of that age do not go quietly
annotations.label: Personification with a negative
annotations.why: A short abstract subject plus a human verb reads as confident speech.

annotations.span: draped over the end of the lane
annotations.label: One verb replaces a clause
annotations.why: 'Draped' carries exhaustion and posture together in a single word.

annotations.span: I did something irreversible to a knee
annotations.label: Precision through vagueness
annotations.why: Naming the effect rather than the injury sounds like real speech.

annotations.span: what I'd actually have recovered is the hour, rather than the distance
annotations.label: Reframes the goal at the close
annotations.why: Ending by correcting your own stated aim is the strongest finish available.

I would like to speak about my hobby, it is repairing old bicycles. I do this since eleven years.

I start because my neighbour is leaving one bicycle in our shed when he moved away. It was very old and it was broken, and I don't know anything about bicycles. But I watched some videos and I try. After two months it was working, and this was a very good feeling for me.

model_answers.transcript:
The hobby I'd talk about is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been doing for about eleven years now.

It started more or less by accident. A neighbour moved out and left a bicycle in our shed — a heavy old thing with a bent wheel and no brakes to speak of — and rather than take it to the tip I decided I'd have a look at it. I knew nothing whatsoever about bicycles at that point. It took me two months, a great many internet videos and one very patient man in a bike shop, but eventually the thing worked. The back wheel alone took three separate attempts. I'm not sure I've been that pleased with myself since.

These days it's a Sunday morning job. A couple of hours most weeks, more if something's genuinely stuck. I pick bikes up cheaply, do them up over a month or two, and then give them away — I've handed on four so far, which is a good deal more satisfying than selling them would be. None of them costs more than about thirty pounds to start with.

The reason it's survived when other things haven't is that it's the exact opposite of my job. At work nothing is ever really finished and half the problems belong to somebody else. Whereas a bent wheel is a bent wheel. It's in front of you, it's yours, and when it's straight you can see that it's straight. That sounds like a small thing, and eleven years suggests otherwise.

annotations.label: Three things, rising
annotations.why: Put the funniest or oddest item last and the list lands.

annotations.label: The exact phrasal verb
annotations.why: 'Do up' is what people actually say about restoring old things.

annotations.why: Name what fell away and this bullet answers itself.

model_answers.transcript:
The one that's lasted is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been at for something like eleven years.

It began by accident, as most of these things do. A neighbour moved out and abandoned a bicycle in our shed — heavy, bent wheel, brakes in name only — and instead of taking it to the tip I thought I'd see what could be done with it. I knew absolutely nothing. Two months, an unreasonable number of videos and one extremely patient man in a bike shop later, the thing rode. The back wheel alone took three goes. I don't think I've been quite so pleased with myself before or since.

It's a Sunday morning habit now. Two hours most weeks, longer when something refuses to move. I buy them cheaply, work on them across a month or so, and then hand them on — four have gone to friends, which beats selling them by a distance I can't really explain. Nothing I buy costs more than about thirty pounds.

What's kept it going, when so much else has fallen by the wayside, is that it is the precise inverse of my working life. At work, nothing concludes and half of every problem belongs to somebody down the corridor. A bent wheel, on the other hand, is a bent wheel. It sits in front of you, it belongs to nobody else, and when you have straightened it, it is visibly straight and it is done.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe one tradition of my country that I did it. It is a bread day in the village of my aunt, before the spring holiday.

The village is small, maybe four hours from my city. All the families bring the dough to one big oven and they cook the bread together. This oven is very old, I think more than one hundred years.

I go there when I was twenty-two. Before that I always say no, because it is early and it is boring for me. But my mother asked me many times, so I went.

We arrive at six in the morning and there is already a queue. I had to make the dough with my hands for one hour, and my arms were killing me. Then you must make the shape, and my shape was very bad, everybody was laughing.

In that moment I felt embarrassed and I want to go home. But now when I think about it, I feel different. It was nice to do something that my grandmother also did. So this is the tradition that I took part in it.

model_answers.label: The same morning at band 7
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd describe is a bread-baking morning that happens in my aunt's village every spring, the day before the main holiday. Every family brings their dough down to one communal oven and the whole thing gets baked together.

The village is tiny — four hours from where I grew up, three streets and an oven that's supposedly two hundred years old. I'd been going there as a child and doing absolutely nothing, and I finally took part properly when I was twenty-two. Until then I'd always found a reason not to. It starts at five in the morning, which was most of the reason.

By the time we got there at six the queue was already halfway down the lane. My job turned out to be kneading for the best part of an hour, which sounds straightforward and is not. After that you shape the loaves, and mine came out looking like something a child had made. The woman next to me rearranged two of them without saying anything at all, which was somehow worse than a comment. The oven itself was too hot to stand anywhere near for long.

At the time I was mortified, and I spent the walk back working out how soon I could reasonably leave. Looking back, though, I'm oddly glad about the whole thing. Not because of the bread, which was ordinary. It was more that my grandmother had stood in that queue, and until that morning that had been a story rather than something I'd done.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect twice for backshift, and past continuous holding the background.
'Found a reason not to', 'mortified', 'somehow worse than a comment' — precise.
The feeling is split into then and now, which is what the fourth bullet asks for.

annotations.why: Two concrete nouns and a number put the listener in the village.

annotations.span: I'd been going there as a child and doing absolutely nothing
annotations.label: Perfect continuous for the years before

annotations.span: Until then I'd always found a reason not to.

annotations.label: Shows the judgement, doesn't state it

annotations.span: At the time I was mortified
annotations.label: One word instead of three
annotations.why: 'Mortified' says badly embarrassed and is worth having ready.

annotations.span: Looking back, though, I'm oddly glad about the whole thing.

model_answers.label: The top of the range
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd describe is a bread morning in my aunt's village, held the day before the main spring holiday, when every household carries its dough down to one shared oven and the lot goes in together.

The village amounts to three streets and that oven, which is said to be two hundred years old and probably isn't. I'd been taken there every year as a child and had contributed nothing whatsoever. Not until I was twenty-two did I actually take part, largely because the thing begins at five in the morning and I had spent a decade finding that unanswerable.

We arrived at six to find the queue already halfway down the lane. My allotted job was kneading, for something close to an hour, which sounds undemanding and is the opposite of it. The dough had been sitting under a cloth in the back of the car since four. Then came the shaping, at which I was conspicuously poor. The woman beside me quietly reshaped two of my loaves and said nothing, which stung considerably more than criticism would have. None of it had been explained to me; you were simply expected to watch.

I was mortified at the time and spent the walk back calculating how early I could decently leave. What I feel now is harder to name. The bread itself was unremarkable. But my grandmother had queued in that lane, and up to that morning that had been a piece of family furniture rather than anything I had physically done.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion after 'not until', against band 7's plain statement order.
'Conspicuously poor', 'stung', 'family furniture' — chosen for shade, not size.
The close admits the feeling is hard to name instead of tidying it away.

annotations.label: Negative inversion
annotations.why: Front 'not until' and invert the subject and auxiliary — one sentence lifts the register.

annotations.span: which is said to be two hundred years old and probably isn't
annotations.label: Reported passive, then a flat denial
annotations.why: 'Is said to be' lets you report a claim without owning it.

annotations.span: which stung considerably more than criticism would have
annotations.label: A verb doing emotional work
annotations.why: 'Stung' carries the feeling that three adjectives would only approximate.

annotations.span: a piece of family furniture
annotations.label: Metaphor made from plain words
annotations.why: Ordinary vocabulary in an unexpected pairing outperforms any rare word.

annotations.span: What I feel now is harder to name.
annotations.label: Refuses the tidy answer
annotations.why: Admitting the feeling is complicated reads as honesty, not as hesitation.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a decision I made about three years ago. At that time I am working in a small company, only nine people, and another company offered me a job.

The other job was better. The salary was more, maybe twenty percent more, and the office was near to my home, only twenty minutes. So it was a good offer, and everybody told me to take it. My mother said take it, my friends said take it also.

But I decided to stay in my company. Because in my company I have a manager and she is very good, she teaches me many things. And in the big company I don't know anybody, and I think maybe I am only a number for them.

So I said no to them. It was difficult, and for two months I feel bad about the money. But after six months my manager gives me a big project alone, and now I am a team leader. So it was good. If I take that job, maybe I am not a team leader now. So I think money is not everything, and this is my decision that turned out well.

what_caps_it.point: Almost every sentence opens with 'so', 'and' or 'but', and the close repeats the card.
The story slides into the present four times and the conditional never gets built.
'Good', 'better', 'big', 'difficult' — the entire judgement runs on four flat adjectives.

annotations.span: about three years ago
annotations.label: Fixes the time in sentence one
annotations.why: Keep this — one time phrase up front is what the whole tense hangs on.

annotations.span: I want to tell about a decision
annotations.label: Wrong verb pattern with 'tell'
annotations.why: Say 'I'd like to talk about a decision'. You tell someone something, not about something.

annotations.span: At that time I am working in a small company
annotations.label: Story slips out of the past
annotations.why: 'At that time I was working' — set the tense here and it holds for two minutes.

annotations.span: So it was good.
annotations.label: Flat evaluation where the marks are
annotations.why: Swap for 'it worked out better than I expected' or 'it opened something up'.

annotations.span: If I take that job, maybe I am not a team leader now.
annotations.label: Conditional collapses into the present
annotations.why: Say 'If I'd taken that job, I wouldn't be a team leader now.'

annotations.span: this is my decision that turned out well
annotations.label: Closes by reading the card back
annotations.why: Close on a thought about decisions, not on the wording of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a decision I made about three years ago, which was turning down a job that would have paid me quite a bit more.

At the time I was working for a small firm — nine of us, all in one room — and a much bigger company got in touch and offered me a role. On paper it was an easy call. The salary was around twenty per cent higher, the office was twenty minutes from my flat rather than an hour, and not one person I asked told me to stay.

What made me hesitate was my manager. She'd taught me most of what I actually know how to do, and she was still handing me work I wasn't quite ready for, which is how you learn anything. At the bigger place I'd have been one of about forty people doing the same job. So it came down to money against the person I was learning from, and in the end that's what tipped the balance.

Turning it down was harder than I expected, and for the first couple of months I did wonder whether I'd been sentimental about it. Then, about six months later, she put me in charge of a project on my own, and I'm now running a small team, whereas if I'd moved I'd probably still be doing the same tasks I was doing back then. Looking back, I'd say the useful part wasn't the decision itself — it was working out that I was choosing what I'd be taught, not just where I'd sit.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect, a 'would have' and a mixed conditional replace the flat run of past simples.
'On paper', 'tipped the balance', 'got in touch' — chunks carry the meaning, not adjectives.
Two signposted moves, and a close that names what was learned rather than the card.

annotations.span: I'll talk about a decision I made about three years ago
annotations.label: Fixes the time frame immediately
annotations.why: One time phrase up front locks the entire answer into the past.

annotations.span: On paper it was an easy call.
annotations.label: Two chunks in one short sentence
annotations.why: Reuse 'on paper' whenever the obvious answer turned out to be wrong.

annotations.span: What made me hesitate was my manager.
annotations.label: Cleft sentence announces the turn
annotations.why: 'What made me ___ was ___' buys you a whole clause of thinking time.

annotations.span: She'd taught me most of what I actually know how to do
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the background
annotations.why: Use it once per story to show two layers of time.

annotations.span: that's what tipped the balance
annotations.label: The exact idiom for a close choice
annotations.why: Keep it for any decision question, in Part 1 or Part 3.

annotations.span: I did wonder whether I'd been sentimental about it
annotations.label: Admits a doubt instead of a clean story
annotations.why: One reservation makes the whole account sound remembered rather than prepared.

annotations.span: and I'm now running a small team, whereas
annotations.label: Contrast joined with 'whereas', not 'but'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' links two full clauses and marks the comparison as deliberate.

annotations.span: if I'd moved I'd probably still be doing the same tasks
annotations.label: Mixed conditional — past cause, present result
annotations.why: This is the natural structure whenever you judge an old decision.

annotations.span: Looking back, I'd say the useful part wasn't the decision itself
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluation out loud
annotations.why: Naming the move stops you drifting past the 'explain' bullet.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
This was three years ago, and it was a decision to turn something down rather than to take it — an offer that was, on the face of it, plainly better than what I already had.

I was at a small firm then, nine of us in a single room, and a far larger company approached me. Twenty per cent more money, a twenty-minute commute instead of an hour, and not one person I consulted advised me against it. What nobody could see from outside was that most of the value of the job I was in sat with one person — the manager who'd trained me, and who was still quietly handing me work I hadn't earned yet. That is a rare thing, and it isn't advertised anywhere.

So the choice wasn't really money against loyalty. It was whether I was picking a salary or picking who I'd be taught by, and once I'd put it in those terms it more or less made itself.

It was still uncomfortable. For a couple of months I half-suspected I'd dressed up cold feet as principle. Then, six months in, she handed me a project of my own, and I've run a small team ever since. Had I taken the offer, I'd almost certainly have ended up competent and interchangeable, which is a worse place to be at that age than underpaid. What I take from it now is that the decisions people call good ones are rarely the ones with the better numbers attached — they're the ones where somebody managed to work out what they were actually choosing between.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion — 'Had I taken the offer' — replaces the standard conditional band 7 used.
'On the face of it', 'dressed up cold feet as principle' — idiom placed, not displayed.
The close generalises about decisions rather than summing this one up.

annotations.span: on the face of it
annotations.label: Idiom used where a native would
annotations.why: Two natural idioms in two minutes beat five decorative ones.

annotations.span: Twenty per cent more money, a twenty-minute commute instead of an hour, and not one person I consulted advised me against it.
annotations.label: A list run as one rhythmic sweep
annotations.why: Keep pitch level across the items and fall only on the last one.

annotations.span: It was whether I was picking a salary or picking who I'd be taught by
annotations.label: Reframes the choice instead of restating it
annotations.why: Saying what the decision was really between is worth more than more detail.

annotations.span: I'd dressed up cold feet as principle
annotations.label: One precise phrase does the self-criticism
annotations.why: Choosing the exact words beats stacking on rare vocabulary.

annotations.span: Had I taken the offer
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, higher register, still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: they're the ones where somebody managed to work out what they were actually choosing between
annotations.label: Lands on a general claim
annotations.why: Ending above the anecdote lifts the whole turn out of storytelling.

part3_themes.title: how people weigh up a choice
questions: Why do some people find even small decisions difficult?
What makes somebody good at deciding things?
Do people where you live tend to decide on their own, or with the family?
part3_themes.counterpoint: most people don't weigh anything up — they decide on instinct and then invent the reasons afterwards

part3_themes.concession_frame: There's a lot in that — although I'd still say ___

question_notes.watch_out: Don't list five causes. Take two and rank them out loud.

question_notes.answer_shape: Give the criterion first, then one example of somebody who meets it.
question_notes.probe: Is that a skill or a temperament?
question_notes.watch_out: Answer 'what makes' with a quality, not with a story about a person.

question_notes.answer_shape: State the tendency with a quantifier, then name one situation that reverses it.
question_notes.watch_out: Say 'most families here', not the bare word 'people'.

part3_themes.title: having far more options than before
questions: Do people today have too many choices to make?
How is choosing a career different now from in your parents' time?

part3_themes.counter_probe: Isn't that a complaint only people with options get to make?
part3_themes.concession_frame: That's a fair point — even so, ___

abstraction_ladder.concrete: Do you find it harder to choose when there's a lot on offer?
abstraction_ladder.local_general: Do people you know put off decisions more than they used to?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: Is there a level of choice beyond which a society stops benefiting from it?

question_notes.answer_shape: Concede the benefit, name the cost, then say which side you come down on.
question_notes.watch_out: Don't answer with a list of choices. Take a position and defend it.

question_notes.answer_shape: Compare with your parents' generation, name what changed, then say why.
question_notes.watch_out: Use 'used to' once — it is the natural form and it earns grammar credit.

question_notes.answer_shape: Predict, hedge the prediction, then name the one decision people will keep.
question_notes.watch_out: Bare 'will' sounds certain — pair it with 'I'd imagine' or 'is likely to'.

teaching.band_move: Answer the question you were asked before widening it. Don't reach for the abstract version first.
teaching.bridge: You've told me about one decision of your own. I'd like to move on now and think about how people make choices more generally.

error_watchlist.wrong: The number of choices people face are enormous now.
error_watchlist.right: The number of choices people face is enormous now.
error_watchlist.why: The verb belongs to 'number', not to 'choices'.

error_watchlist.wrong: The young people today decide everything alone.
error_watchlist.right: Young people today decide everything on their own.
error_watchlist.why: Plural generalisations take no article at all.

questions: Whereabouts is your home town?
How often do you get back there these days?
Was it much the same when you were a child?
Is it the sort of place people want to move to?
If you could change one thing about it, what would it be?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple for the place, past simple for childhood, second conditional for the last question
teaching.band_move: Locate the place before you describe it — a country and a direction cost you four words.

questions.answer_shape: Country, then a direction or a nearby city, then one size detail.
questions.extend_move: It's a fairly small town in the north, about an hour inland from the coast.

common_error.wrong: It is in the north of the my country.
common_error.right: It's in the north of the country.
common_error.why: Never stack 'the' and a possessive together.

questions.probe: Is that where you live now?

questions.answer_shape: Say how often, then when you last went and why.
questions.extend_move: Every couple of months — more if there's something on at my parents' place.

common_error.wrong: I go there each two months.
common_error.right: I go there every couple of months.
common_error.why: 'Every', not 'each', with a number and a plural.

questions.answer_shape: Say what's the same, then name one thing that isn't.
questions.extend_move: Broadly, yes, though the whole waterfront was rebuilt about ten years ago.

common_error.wrong: When I am a child, the town was smaller.
common_error.right: When I was a child, the town was smaller.
common_error.why: Both halves of a past sentence take past tense.

questions.answer_shape: Generalise with a quantifier, then say who exactly it suits.
questions.extend_move: Not really — a fair few people leave at eighteen and come back at forty, if at all.

common_error.wrong: The people don't like to live in small towns.
common_error.right: Most people don't want to live in small towns.
common_error.why: Plural generalisations take no article.

questions.answer_shape: Name one thing, use 'I'd', then say what difference it would make.
questions.extend_move: I'd put a decent train service in — everything else follows from being able to get out.

common_error.wrong: If I can change, I will build more parks.
common_error.right: If I could change one thing, I'd build more parks.
common_error.why: Imaginary situations take 'could' plus 'would'.

questions: How many hours do you tend to sleep?
Are you better first thing in the morning or late at night?
Did you sleep more when you were younger?
Do people where you live generally get enough sleep?
Is there anything about your sleep you'd like to change?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple with frequency adverbs, past simple for childhood, 'would' for the change
teaching.band_move: Put the frequency adverb before the main verb, every time — it is the highest-density slip in this frame.

questions.answer_shape: Give a number, then say whether that's enough for you.
questions.extend_move: About six and a half on a weeknight, which isn't really enough, if I'm honest.

common_error.wrong: I sleep usually seven hours.
common_error.right: I usually sleep about seven hours.
common_error.why: Frequency adverbs come before the main verb.

questions.probe: Is it the same at weekends?

questions.answer_shape: Pick one, give the reason, then concede what you lose by it.
questions.extend_move: Late at night, easily — I get more done after ten than I do all afternoon.

common_error.wrong: I am more better in the night.
common_error.right: I'm much better at night.
common_error.why: Never put 'more' in front of an -er form.

questions.answer_shape: Past simple or 'used to', one example, then contrast with now.
questions.extend_move: Far more — I used to sleep until midday at weekends and think nothing of it.

common_error.wrong: I was sleeping more when I am young.
common_error.right: I slept a lot more when I was younger.
common_error.why: Past habits take past simple or 'used to'.

questions.answer_shape: Use a quantifier, name the cause, then give one exception.
questions.extend_move: Most people I know don't — the commuting alone takes two hours out of the day.

common_error.wrong: In my country peoples sleep very less.
common_error.right: Where I live, people don't sleep much.
common_error.why: 'People' is already plural and 'less' needs a noun.

questions.answer_shape: Name the change, use 'I'd', then say what's stopping you.
questions.extend_move: I'd like to get up earlier, but I'd have to give up the evenings to do it.

common_error.wrong: I want to sleep early but I can't to do it.
common_error.right: I'd like to go to bed earlier, but I can't seem to.

title: An important change you have made in your life

payload_json.topic: An important change you have made in your life

cue_card.topic: Describe an important change you have made in your life.
bullets: what the change was
when you made it
who else it affected
and explain what difference it has made to you.
rounding_off: Did other people notice the change in you?
Would it have been easier to do earlier?

teaching.band_move: Build a visible before and after: one past perfect for the years before, past simple for the moment itself.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Choose a change you made on purpose, not one that happened to you. Moving, quitting, starting something — whatever you can date.

note_grid.cell: closer to them now, see 1x wk

prep_plan.trap: People spend the whole turn on the before and never say what is actually different now.

time_plan.goal: Name the change and roughly when.
How things stood before, and the moment.
Who else it landed on, and how.
The difference — expected and unexpected.
One line about change in general.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe the new place or situation — size, cost, what you could see from it.
Add time depth: say how long you'd been thinking about it before you acted.
Bring somebody in: report what one family member actually said to you.
Evaluate aloud: say whether you'd advise somebody else to do the same.

error_watchlist.wrong: Before, I am living with my parents and everything is done for me.
error_watchlist.right: Before that, I was living with my parents and everything was done for me.
error_watchlist.why: Fix the tense in the first clause and hold it.

error_watchlist.wrong: Now I am more independent person.
error_watchlist.right: I'm a more independent person now.
error_watchlist.why: A singular countable noun always needs a determiner.

error_watchlist.wrong: I moved out from my parents' house to other side of the city.
error_watchlist.right: I moved out of my parents' house to the other side of the city.
error_watchlist.why: Learn 'move out of' as one chunk.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: This card is thick with clusters, and a dropped one takes the grammar down with it.

target_words.note: Three sounds at the end — don't reduce it to 'muns'.
Keep the /skt/; 'ast' sounds like a different tense.
The /d/ survives before the /st/.
Both consonants at the front: /ks/ then /p/.
Don't drop the /d/ before the /m/.

chunking_drill.sentence: It's one room and a kitchen, and the rent takes a third of what I earn, but it's mine.
chunks: It's one room and a kitchen,
and the rent takes a third of what I earn,

minimal_pairs.contrast: the plural adds a cluster most learners drop entirely

teaching.examiner_note: You get the card, paper and a pencil, and exactly one minute. The examiner will not answer a question about the card during that minute.

swap_slots.prompt: Your own timing. A season and a year is plenty — resist giving an exact date.

swap_slots.span: my parents, my two sisters and my grandmother, all in one house
swap_slots.prompt: Who you actually lived with, counted. A number makes it yours; 'my family' does not.

swap_slots.prompt: One concrete fact about the new situation — distance, rent, size. Pick the one you can picture.
