model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my aunt. She is the sister of my father and she has a small bakery in our town.

She gave me a very useful advice when I was twenty years old. At that time I have a problem because I got a job offer and also I got a place in a course, and I don't know what to choose. So I asked everybody, my parents, my friends, my old teacher. Everybody said something different, so after that it was more confusing for me than before.

Then one day I was in her kitchen and I am telling her about this problem again. And she said, take a paper and write the answer that you already choose. Just write it. So I wrote it and it was the course. I wrote it very fast, without thinking.

Then she said, so you are not confused, you only want somebody to say it is okay. And this was true. So I took the course and I never regret it. She is a very practical person and this is why her advice was so useful for me.

what_caps_it.point: 'Advice' is treated as countable, and 'useful' and 'practical' carry every judgement.
'I have a problem' and 'I am telling her' sit inside a past narrative.
The turn closes on the prompt's own words and never says what changed afterwards.

annotations.span: Then one day I was in her kitchen
annotations.label: Anchors the moment in a place
annotations.why: A place and a time make an examiner hear an event rather than a summary.

annotations.span: She gave me a very useful advice
annotations.label: 'Advice' is uncountable
annotations.why: Say 'a very useful piece of advice'. There is no 'an advice'.

annotations.span: At that time I have a problem
annotations.label: Present tense in a past story
annotations.why: Fix the tense in the first sentence and keep it for two whole minutes.

annotations.span: I am telling her about this problem again
annotations.label: Continuous where past simple belongs
annotations.why: Use 'I was telling her' for background only; the event itself is past simple.

annotations.span: She is a very practical person and this is why her advice was so useful for me.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: End on what the advice changed, never by repeating the card's own words.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one who comes to mind is my father's sister, who runs a small bakery in the town I grew up in. She's not somebody I'd have thought of as an adviser, which is probably why it worked.

This was when I was about twenty. I'd been offered a job and I'd also been given a place on a course, and the two of them started within a fortnight of each other. I asked everybody I could think of, and every single one of them had a different opinion, so by the end of that I was considerably less clear than when I started. That went on for the better part of three weeks.

I was sitting in her kitchen going over the whole thing yet again when she stopped me. She pushed a piece of paper across the table and said, write down the one you've already chosen. Not the one you should choose. The one you've already chosen. I wrote 'course' without thinking about it at all, which took roughly two seconds. She didn't even look up while I was writing.

And then she said the thing I still repeat to people: you're not undecided, you just want somebody to tell you it's all right. That was exactly what had been going on. I'd been collecting opinions rather than weighing anything up, because the choice had already been made and I hadn't admitted it. The useful part, in hindsight, wasn't the advice. It was being told what I was actually doing.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect carries the background layer, including 'I hadn't admitted it' at the close.
'Going over the whole thing', 'weighing anything up' and 'collecting opinions' do the evaluating.
The quoted line is set up, delivered and then interpreted, so the point lands twice.

annotations.span: She's not somebody I'd have thought of as an adviser, which is probably why it worked.
annotations.label: Frames the person before the story
annotations.why: One line of judgement up front tells the listener what to watch for.

annotations.span: I'd been offered a job and I'd also been given a place on a course
annotations.label: Passive past perfect, used twice
annotations.why: Two things already true before the story starts belong in the past perfect.

annotations.span: I was sitting in her kitchen going over the whole thing yet again when she stopped me.
annotations.label: Continuous background, simple event
annotations.why: Set the scene in continuous, then interrupt it with a past simple verb.

annotations.span: She pushed a piece of paper across the table and said, write down the one you've already chosen.
annotations.label: Reports the gesture and the words
annotations.why: Give what they did as well as what they said; it doubles the detail for free.

annotations.span: weighing anything up
annotations.label: A phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: Reuse it for any decision where two sides have to be compared.

annotations.span: And then she said the thing I still repeat to people
annotations.label: Signals the key line is coming
annotations.why: Flagging the important sentence makes a listener slow down for it.

annotations.span: I'd been collecting opinions
annotations.label: Names the behaviour in two words
annotations.why: A precise verb replaces a whole sentence of explanation.

annotations.span: Not the one you should choose. The one you've already chosen.
annotations.label: Stress on 'should', then 'already'
annotations.why: The whole point is a contrast; unstressed, a listener just hears a repeat.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd point to is my father's sister. She runs a bakery, has never given a lecture in her life, and is the only person whose advice I have ever acted on immediately.

I was twenty and stuck between a job and a place on a course, both of them starting inside a fortnight. In the weeks before that, I had consulted, by my own count, nine separate people. All nine were confident, none of them agreed, and the net effect was that I understood the choice rather less well than before I began. It is a peculiar kind of paralysis, and I would not recommend it to anybody.

She listened to about four minutes of it in her kitchen and then slid a sheet of paper across the table. Write down the one you have already picked, she said. Not the sensible one. The one you have already picked. I wrote it in about two seconds, which was itself the answer.

Then came the line I have been quoting ever since: you are not undecided, you simply want permission. She was entirely right. What I had been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a decision I had made weeks earlier and could not own. Rarely have I been read that accurately by anybody. And I think the lesson generalises: the most useful people are not the ones who tell you what to do, but the ones who describe what you are doing.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Rarely have I been' inverts, and the past perfect runs the entire background layer.
'Canvassing', 'ratified' and 'slid a sheet of paper' are chosen for exactness, not effect.
The close turns the anecdote into a claim about what useful people actually do.

annotations.span: Rarely have I been read that accurately by anybody.
annotations.label: Adverb fronting with inversion
annotations.why: Put the negative adverb first and invert; it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: What I had been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a decision I had made weeks earlier
annotations.label: Cleft over a past perfect continuous
annotations.why: Two structures at once, both accurate: that is what band 8 sounds like.

annotations.span: the net effect was that I understood the choice rather less well than before I began
annotations.label: Precise rather than decorative
annotations.why: State the size of the effect and you never need the word 'confusing'.

annotations.span: you simply want permission
annotations.label: One noun replaces a paragraph
annotations.why: Find the abstract noun for a behaviour and the sentence shortens itself.

annotations.span: not the ones who tell you what to do, but the ones who describe what you are doing
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Abstract in the final clause and the turn stops being just an anecdote.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a woman who I met one time on a bus. It was a night bus and I never see her again after that.

It was about seven years ago. I was travelling to another city for a job interview and the bus was broken. So we stopped at a service station in the middle of the night and we waited there for four hours. It was very cold and there was nothing to do, all the shops are closed.

She was sitting next to me. She was around sixty years old, I think. She was going to a hospital in the same city because she had an appointment in the morning. We started to talk and then we talked until five o'clock. She asked me many questions about my life, my family, my job. Nobody asks me these questions normally, even my friends.

The strange thing is I don't know her name. I never ask her and she never ask me. When the new bus came we sat in different seats and that was all. But I still remember her and sometimes I use her questions with other people. So this is a person I met one time and I still remember.

what_caps_it.point: The present tense keeps intruding, and 'the bus was broken' should be a breakdown.
Everything is joined with 'and' or 'so', and the striking part arrives completely flat.
'Strange', 'cold' and 'many questions' are the only descriptive choices in the turn.

annotations.span: It was about seven years ago.
annotations.label: Fixes the time in five words
annotations.why: Keep this. One time phrase up front locks the whole answer into the past.

annotations.span: I never see her again after that
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'I never saw her again'. Choose the tense once and hold it.

annotations.span: the bus was broken
annotations.label: Wrong verb for a breakdown
annotations.why: A vehicle 'breaks down'; 'was broken' describes a permanent state.

annotations.span: I never ask her and she never ask me.
annotations.label: Past tense missing twice over
annotations.why: Say 'I never asked her and she never asked me'.

annotations.span: So this is a person I met one time and I still remember.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's own words
annotations.why: End on why brief encounters stay with people at all.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd like to describe is somebody whose name I never actually found out, which is part of why she stuck.

This was about seven years ago. I was on an overnight coach to another city for an interview, and the coach broke down at around midnight. They pulled us into a service station and we sat there for something like four hours, in the cold, with nothing open. I'd been half asleep until then, so I was fairly annoyed about the whole thing.

She was in the seat across the aisle, a woman in her sixties, travelling to a hospital appointment first thing the next morning. I don't remember how we got chatting, but once we did we talked more or less until it got light. What I remember most clearly is that she asked far better questions than anybody I knew. Not the usual ones. She asked me what I'd been like at fourteen, and whether the job I was going for was one I actually wanted or one that would look sensible. Nobody had ever put it to me quite like that.

When the replacement coach turned up we ended up in different seats, and that was the end of it. I never asked her name, which I've regretted ever since. What I've kept is the questions. I've used two of them on other people since then, and they work every single time. It's an odd thing to take away from four hours in a car park, but there it is.

what_lifts_it.point: 'I'd been half asleep' and 'Nobody had ever put it' add a second layer of past time.
'Got chatting', 'until it got light' and 'there it is' are spoken rather than written.
One time frame holds for two minutes and the close names what actually survived.

annotations.span: somebody whose name I never actually found out, which is part of why she stuck
annotations.label: Opens on the memorable detail
annotations.why: Put the strangest fact first; it gives the listener a reason to stay.

annotations.span: I'd been half asleep until then
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the earlier state
annotations.why: One backshifted verb shows two layers of time inside a story.

annotations.span: how we got chatting
annotations.label: Spoken chunk, not a formal phrase
annotations.why: 'Get chatting' is what people say; the formal version sounds written.

annotations.span: What I remember most clearly is that
annotations.label: Signposts the important part
annotations.why: Announcing the key detail makes a listener slow down for it.

annotations.span: Not the usual ones.
annotations.label: Short, falling, after a pause
annotations.why: A three-word sentence between long ones controls the rhythm of a turn.

annotations.span: whether the job I was going for was one I actually wanted or one that would look sensible
annotations.label: Embedded question with two options
annotations.why: Embedded questions keep statement order, and getting that right is very audible.

annotations.span: What I've kept is the questions.
annotations.label: Turns the story into a takeaway
annotations.why: Say what survived and the fourth bullet more or less answers itself.

annotations.span: It's an odd thing to take away from four hours in a car park
annotations.label: Understatement does the evaluating
annotations.why: Play a big point down and it lands harder than an intensifier would.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd choose is somebody I spent five hours with and cannot name, which is precisely why she has lasted.

Seven years ago I was on an overnight coach, travelling to an interview in another city, and somewhere around midnight the thing gave out. We were decanted into a service station forecourt and left there for the best part of four hours, in the cold, with everything shut. I had been asleep and was in no mood for any of it.

She was across the aisle. Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, entirely unbothered by the delay. I have no memory of how the conversation started, only that it ran until the sky went grey. What struck me, and still does, is the quality of her questions. She asked what I had been like at fourteen. She asked whether the job I was travelling for was one I wanted, or one that would simply look defensible to other people. I had no answer to the second, which was itself informative.

The relief coach arrived, we were seated separately, and that was that. Not once did it occur to me to ask her name. What I took away was the questions themselves, two of which I have since used on other people to considerable effect. Some of the people who change how you think, it turns out, are people you meet for one night and never see again.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Not once did it occur' inverts, and 'two of which' replaces a whole extra sentence.
'Decanted', 'gave out' and 'look defensible' are each chosen for a shade of meaning.
The close states a general claim about brief encounters instead of summarising the night.

annotations.span: Not once did it occur to me to ask her name.
annotations.label: Negative fronting with inversion
annotations.why: Front the negative and invert; it reads as spoken emphasis, not as writing.

annotations.span: two of which I have since used on other people
annotations.label: Quantifier plus 'of which' relative
annotations.why: It joins two ideas without the extra 'and I have also' sentence.

annotations.span: We were decanted into a service station forecourt
annotations.label: One precise verb, faintly dry
annotations.why: The exact verb carries the tone as well as the meaning.

annotations.span: one that would simply look defensible to other people
annotations.label: Names the real motive precisely
annotations.why: Choosing 'defensible' over 'good' is the shade of meaning band 8 rewards.

annotations.span: Some of the people who change how you think, it turns out, are people you meet for one night
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Abstract in the last sentence and the whole turn stops being anecdote.

annotations.span: Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, entirely unbothered by the delay.
annotations.label: Three groups, one falling contour
annotations.why: Keep a list level in pitch and drop only on the final group.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time I explained something difficult. It was to my grandmother and it was about her bank.

Last year her bank closed the branch in her town and they said everything is on the app now. She is eighty-one and she never used a smartphone before. My uncle explained her two times and the bank explained also, but she doesn't understand anything. She was very worried, she thought maybe her money is gone.

So I went to her house on a Sunday. First I show her the app, step by step, this button, then this button. But it was not working. She was more confused than before. Then I stopped and I asked her, what do you think happens with your money. And she said, it is in the building. She thought the money is physically inside the branch, like in a box.

So then I took a paper and I drew it. The bank, the computer, and the money is only a number. After that it was easy, in ten minutes she was fine.

I felt happy but also stupid, because I explained one hour the wrong thing. So this is the time I explained something difficult.

what_caps_it.point: The present tense keeps returning inside a past story, and reported speech never shifts.
'So' opens four sentences, and the key realisation arrives with no build-up at all.
'Difficult', 'confused', 'easy' and 'happy' do all of the evaluation between them.

annotations.why: Keep this. Quoting the question you asked is the strongest moment in the turn.

annotations.label: Reported speech doesn't shift back

annotations.why: Decide on the past in your opening line and never drift out.

model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick is explaining online banking to my grandmother, which sounds trivial and absolutely was not.

Her local branch shut about a year ago and the bank moved more or less everything onto an app. She's eighty-one and had never owned a smartphone. By the time I got involved, my uncle had been through it with her twice and somebody at the bank had tried as well, and none of it had landed. What worried me was that she'd started saying she no longer knew where her money was, which is not a small thing to be thinking at eighty-one.

I went round on a Sunday and did exactly what everybody else had done. I opened the app and walked her through it, screen by screen. Twenty minutes in, it was clear this was going nowhere, so I stopped and asked her what she thought actually happened to her money when she paid it in. And she said it stayed in the building.

That was the whole problem. In fairness, it was an obvious thing to have checked. She wasn't confused about the app at all; she was confused about where money lives. So I drew it on the back of an envelope, the branch on one side and a number in a computer on the other. After that the app itself took about ten minutes.

What I took from it is that most failed explanations are answers to the wrong question. If I'd asked first instead of explaining first, I'd have saved us both an hour.

what_lifts_it.point: The past perfect runs the whole background, and a third conditional closes the reflection.
'None of it had landed', 'going nowhere' and 'where money lives' are precise and spoken.
The discovery is withheld until the right moment, so the explanation has a visible shape.

annotations.label: Frames the story before telling it
annotations.why: Warning a listener that it gets harder buys their attention for nothing.

annotations.span: my uncle had been through it with her twice and somebody at the bank had tried as well
annotations.label: Past perfect for what came before
annotations.why: Everything that happened before your story starts belongs in past perfect.

annotations.span: none of it had landed
annotations.label: One verb for 'she didn't understand'
annotations.why: 'Land' is what people say about explanations that fail. Reuse it.

annotations.span: I went round on a Sunday and did exactly what everybody else had done.
annotations.label: Admits the wrong turn out loud
annotations.why: Naming your own mistake is what turns an anecdote into reasoning.

annotations.span: asked her what she thought actually happened to her money
annotations.label: Embedded question keeps statement order
annotations.why: Not 'what did she think happened'. This one is very visible to examiners.

annotations.span: That was the whole problem.
annotations.label: Marks the discovery in four words
annotations.why: A short sentence after a long one tells a listener something has changed.

annotations.span: she was confused about where money lives
annotations.label: An abstract idea in ordinary words
annotations.why: Saying the difficult thing simply demonstrates the very skill you're describing.

annotations.span: If I'd asked first instead of explaining first, I'd have saved us both an hour.
annotations.label: Third conditional carries the lesson
annotations.why: Any 'what would you change' bullet wants an unreal past somewhere in it.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The episode I'd choose is teaching my grandmother to bank on a phone, which I had assumed would take about twenty minutes.

Her branch closed last year and the bank shifted everything onto an app. She is eighty-one and had never held a smartphone. Two people had already attempted it before me, my uncle and somebody at the counter, and both attempts had sunk without trace. The detail that alarmed me was a remark she made about no longer knowing where her money was, which at eighty-one is not a small sentence.

I went round on the Sunday and proceeded to repeat everybody else's mistake. I opened the application and took her through it screen by screen, patiently and uselessly, for the better part of an hour. Only when I gave up did I think to ask what she believed happened to money once she had handed it over the counter. It stayed in the building, she said. She offered this without a trace of hesitation.

There was the entire problem. The obstacle was never the interface; it was a model of banking formed in about 1960 and never revised since. Two minutes with a pen and an envelope sorted it, and the app followed in ten.

What that taught me has outlasted the banking. Almost every explanation that fails is a well-constructed answer to a question nobody asked. Had I begun by finding out what she already believed, I would have saved us both the hour.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Only when I gave up did I think' and 'Had I begun' put two inversions into one turn.
'Sunk without trace', 'patiently and uselessly' and 'never revised' each carry a judgement.
It closes on a general principle about explanation rather than on the grandmother.

annotations.span: Only when I gave up did I think to ask
annotations.label: Fronted 'only when' forces inversion
annotations.why: It marks the turning point grammatically as well as in the content.

annotations.span: Had I begun by finding out what she already believed
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as a third conditional, one register higher, still spoken.

annotations.span: both attempts had sunk without trace
annotations.label: Idiom exactly where it belongs
annotations.why: Idiom counts when it is invisible; showy ones cost more than they earn.

annotations.span: a model of banking formed in about 1960 and never revised since
annotations.label: Names the real obstacle precisely
annotations.why: Diagnose in a noun phrase and you save yourself three whole sentences.

annotations.span: patiently and uselessly
annotations.label: The second adverb takes the stress
annotations.why: The contrast between the two words is the point; unstressed, it vanishes.

annotations.span: Almost every explanation that fails is a well-constructed answer to a question nobody asked.
annotations.label: Ends on a general principle
annotations.why: A closing generalisation is what separates a story from an argument.

title: A time you were surprised by someone's kindness

payload_json.topic: A time you were surprised by someone's kindness

cue_card.topic: Describe an occasion when somebody was kinder to you than you expected.
bullets: when and where it happened
who the person was
what they did for you
and explain why it surprised you as much as it did.
rounding_off: Did you ever see that person again?
Would you have done the same in their position?

teaching.band_move: Give the time, the weather and the place in one sentence. An event card needs its scene before its action.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take a small kindness you can date. A large vague one gives you nothing concrete to fill ninety seconds with.

note_grid.cell: no money: 'someone did it for me'

prep_plan.trap: Most people describe the breakdown and forget the person. The card is about her, not about the car.

time_plan.goal: Date the evening and say where you were stuck.
The scene, the wait, then who stopped.
Exactly what she did, with distances and times.
Why the refusal of money changed the meaning.
One line about kindness that travels onwards.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in on the wait: the cold, the dark, what you could actually see.
Say what the hour before had been like, so the rescue registers properly.
Contrast her with the drivers who went past, and be fair to them.
Say what would probably have happened if no van had come along.

error_watchlist.wrong: I was standing there and then a van stops and a woman opens the window.
error_watchlist.right: I was standing there when a van stopped and a woman wound the window down.
error_watchlist.why: Continuous for background, past simple for events.

error_watchlist.wrong: If she doesn't stop, I stay there all night.
error_watchlist.right: If she hadn't stopped, I'd have been there all night.
error_watchlist.why: Both halves go perfect: 'hadn't stopped', 'would have been'.

error_watchlist.wrong: I was waiting since forty minutes in the road.
error_watchlist.right: I'd been waiting for forty minutes at the side of the road.
error_watchlist.why: 'For' takes a length; you wait at the side.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Every verb in this story is past tense, and a swallowed ending reads as a tense error.

target_words.note: One syllable ending in /t/. Never 'stop-ped'.
After a /t/ sound the ending is a whole syllable.
The ending is /d/, blended straight on.
Two syllables, and the ending is a full one.
Two syllables, not three; ending is /d/.

chunks: I stood at the side of the road

minimal_pairs.contrast: the second adds a whole syllable, not just a sound

teaching.examiner_note: Rounding-off questions may be skipped entirely if your talk ran the full two minutes. That is neutral, not a bad sign.

swap_slots.span: about four years ago, in November
swap_slots.prompt: Your own time reference. A season and a year, nothing vaguer than that.

swap_slots.span: The driver was a woman in her fifties
swap_slots.prompt: Your own person. One age and one detail, never a general description.

swap_slots.span: She drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town
swap_slots.prompt: The concrete thing they did, with a number attached to it.

swap_slots.span: I tried to give her something for the petrol

teaching.transfer_drill: Now describe a small kindness you did for somebody else, in exactly the same shape. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a time when somebody was very kind to me. It happened about four years ago in November.

I was driving back from my cousin's house and my car stopped on a small road. It was nine o'clock in the night and it was very dark and cold. I try to call somebody but there was no signal on my phone. So I was waiting there for forty minutes and nobody stopped, maybe three cars passed but they don't stop.

Then a small van stopped. There was a woman inside, maybe fifty years old. She opened the window and she asked me what happened. I explained her about the car. And then she said, get in, I take you to the garage. The garage was twenty kilometres away in another town. She drove me there and she waited also, because it was closed and we must find the man with the key.

After that I want to give her some money but she refused. She said, somebody did this for me before, fifteen years ago. And then she went away. I was very surprised because she doesn't know me at all. So this is the time I was surprised by somebody's kindness.

what_caps_it.point: 'I try', 'they don't stop' and 'I want to give' all sit inside a past narrative.
'Kind', 'surprised' and 'very dark' carry the whole event between them.
A chain of events joined by 'and' and 'so', with the point never actually made.

annotations.span: It happened about four years ago in November.
annotations.label: Dates the event immediately
annotations.why: Keep this. A month and a year lock the whole answer into the past.

annotations.span: I try to call somebody but there was no signal
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'I tried'. Fix the tense once and then hold it throughout.

annotations.span: maybe three cars passed but they don't stop
annotations.label: The tense slips mid-sentence
annotations.why: Both verbs in one sentence must match: 'passed' and 'didn't stop'.

annotations.span: I explained her about the car.
annotations.label: 'Explain' takes 'to'
annotations.why: Say 'I explained the problem to her'. The preposition belongs to the verb.

annotations.span: So this is the time I was surprised by somebody's kindness.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's wording
annotations.why: End on what the evening made you think about strangers.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd choose happened about four years ago, in November, on a completely unremarkable stretch of road.

I'd been at my cousin's and I was driving home when the car simply died. This was somewhere around nine in the evening, in the middle of nowhere, and it turned out there was no signal at all where I'd stopped. I stood at the side of the road for the best part of forty minutes. Three or four cars went past without slowing down, which I honestly don't blame them for, and it was getting properly cold by then. I remember thinking I'd have to walk it.

Then a small van pulled up. The driver was a woman in her fifties, and she wound the window down and asked what had happened. Once I'd explained, she just said get in. She drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, and when it turned out to be shut she waited with me until we'd tracked somebody down. That took another hour, easily.

The part that surprised me was the end of it. I tried to give her something for the petrol and she wouldn't hear of it. All she said was that somebody had done the same for her about fifteen years earlier, and then she drove off before I could ask her anything else at all. I've thought about that a great deal since. It wasn't really kindness towards me at all; it was more like a debt being passed along, and I'm the one holding it now.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect carries the background, including 'until we'd tracked somebody down'.
'Simply died', 'wouldn't hear of it' and 'a debt being passed along' do the evaluating.
The surprise is held back and then explained, so the fourth bullet has somewhere to go.

annotations.span: on a completely unremarkable stretch of road
annotations.label: Sets the scene in six words
annotations.why: One phrase of setting is plenty; a listener fills in all the rest.

annotations.span: I'd been at my cousin's and I was driving home when the car simply died
annotations.label: Three tenses in one sentence
annotations.why: Past perfect, then continuous, then simple: the standard way to open a story.

annotations.span: she wouldn't hear of it
annotations.label: The exact phrase for refusing thanks
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever somebody turns down an offer politely but firmly.

annotations.span: The part that surprised me was the end of it.
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluation bullet
annotations.why: Say the move aloud and the evaluation bullet cannot be forgotten.

annotations.span: somebody had done the same for her about fifteen years earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect inside reported speech
annotations.why: Two steps back in time, and it has to be marked on the verb.

annotations.span: a debt being passed along
annotations.label: One image replaces an explanation
annotations.why: Find the metaphor and five words do the work of three sentences.

annotations.span: It wasn't really kindness towards me at all
annotations.label: Reinterprets the story at the close
annotations.why: Saying what something was not is the cheapest route to a precise point.

annotations.span: That took another hour, easily.
annotations.label: 'Easily' dropped after the pause
annotations.why: A trailing adverb carries understatement that flat delivery loses entirely.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick took place about four years ago on a November evening, on a road with nothing on it in either direction.

I was driving back from my cousin's when the car gave up entirely. Nine o'clock, pitch dark, and of course no signal wherever it was that I had stopped. I stood on the verge for the best part of forty minutes. Several cars came past and not one of them slowed, which in fairness is probably what I would have done myself. It is a long forty minutes when nothing is coming.

Then a small van pulled in. A woman in her fifties, window down, asking what the trouble was. Having heard about thirty seconds of it she told me to get in, drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, found it shut, and then waited with me for another hour while we located somebody with a key.

What has stayed with me is not the lift. It is what she said when I tried to press some money on her for the fuel. She would not take a penny, and remarked, almost in passing, that somebody had done exactly this for her fifteen years earlier. That reframed the whole evening. It had very little to do with me at all; I had simply been handed something that was already in circulation, and at some point I am expected to pass it on.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause opens a sentence, and past perfect handles the fifteen-year backshift.
'Gave up entirely', 'on the verge' and 'already in circulation' are exact, not decorative.
It ends by reframing what happened rather than by summing the evening up.

annotations.span: Having heard about thirty seconds of it she told me to get in
annotations.label: Participle clause compresses a sequence
annotations.why: 'Having done X, she did Y' packs two events into a single clause.

annotations.span: somebody had done exactly this for her fifteen years earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect for a second layer back
annotations.why: Two steps into the past must be marked, or a listener loses the order.

annotations.span: She would not take a penny
annotations.label: Idiomatic refusal, entirely natural
annotations.why: One idiom in the right slot outweighs a handful placed for display.

annotations.span: something that was already in circulation
annotations.label: The metaphor does the whole argument
annotations.why: One well-chosen image replaces a paragraph of explaining.

annotations.span: That reframed the whole evening.
annotations.label: Announces a change of reading
annotations.why: Tell a listener you are about to reinterpret and they follow the shift.

annotations.span: Nine o'clock, pitch dark, and of course no signal
annotations.label: Three groups, one falling run
annotations.why: Group short items at level pitch and fall only on the final one.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about something I do with my family every week. Every Sunday morning we go to the market together.

We are doing this since four years. It started when my father stopped working, because before that he is always busy at the weekend also. Now he have more free time. So every Sunday we wake up early, maybe seven o'clock, and me and my father and my younger brother we walk to the market. It takes twenty minutes to walk there.

At the market we buy the vegetables and the fruit for the week. My father always want to go to the same man because he says his tomatoes are better. My brother says it is the same tomatoes everywhere. So they argue every week about this, it is a joke in our family now. After that we go to a small cafe near there and we drink coffee and we sit maybe one hour.

I like it very much because in the week we don't talk really. We only talk about things like who is taking the car. But on Sunday we talk about normal things. So this is the thing I do with my family regularly.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd describe is a walk to the market that the three of us do every Sunday morning. It's my father, my younger brother and me, and we've been doing it for about four years now.

It started when my father retired. Before that he worked most weekends, so Sunday morning was the first slot in the week that was genuinely free, and I think he wanted something in it. We leave at about seven, which is unreasonable, and walk for twenty minutes or so to the market on the far side of town. None of us has ever suggested going later.

The routine barely varies, which is half the point. We buy the vegetables for the week, my father insists on one particular stall because he maintains the tomatoes there are better, and my brother says every week that tomatoes are tomatoes. They've been having that argument for four years and neither of them has moved an inch. Then we sit in the same café for an hour, in the same three chairs, and nobody's in any hurry about any of it.

What I get out of it isn't really the market. During the week the three of us only ever talk about arrangements: who needs the car, who's collecting what. Sunday is the one stretch where nothing has to be decided. I'd say that's what a routine is actually for. It isn't the activity at all, it's the fact that the time is already booked and nobody has to propose it.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The routine I'd pick is a Sunday-morning walk to the market, done by three of us, and it has been running for roughly four years.

It began, as these things do, when my father retired. Until then he had worked most weekends, so Sunday was the first genuinely unclaimed morning he'd had in decades, and I suspect he wanted it occupied by something. We set off around seven, which nobody has ever formally agreed to, and walk twenty minutes across town in whatever weather happens to be available.

What makes it work is that nothing about it changes. We buy the week's vegetables; my father will not be moved from one particular stall on the grounds that its tomatoes are superior; my brother observes, weekly, that a tomato is a tomato. Four years of this and neither has conceded a millimetre. Neither of them ever will, either. Afterwards there is an hour in the same café, in the same three chairs, and nobody hurries anybody about anything.

The market, though, is not the point. Our weekday conversation consists almost entirely of logistics, who needs the car and who is collecting whom, and Sunday is the only stretch in which nothing at all has to be settled. That, I have come to think, is what a shared routine really provides. Not the activity, but a block of time that has already been agreed, so that nobody ever has to be the one who suggests it.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Will not be moved' as habitual refusal, and 'whom' used where it genuinely belongs.
'Unclaimed', 'conceded a millimetre' and 'observes, weekly' each carry judgement precisely.
The final sentence defines what routines are for rather than restating this one.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe the place where I go when I want to think. It is a canal, behind an old mill building, and it is about fifteen minutes from my house on foot.

So I found it by accident. There was road works on my normal street, so I go a different way, and I see this path next to the water. Before that I don't know it is there, even I live here six years.

Usually I walk maybe twenty minutes and then I sit down. There is a gate on the water, I don't know the English word for this, and I sit on it. Sometimes I take a coffee with me. There is no signal for my phone in this place, so nobody can call me.

It helps me to think because it is very quiet there. In my flat it is not quiet, my neighbours are noisy and there is always something. But there it is only the water and some birds. So my head is more clear and I can think about my problem. It is a very nice place and I feel very relaxed. So this is the quiet place where I go to think.

model_answers.label: The target — same place, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a stretch of canal towpath about fifteen minutes' walk from my flat, tucked away behind an old mill that hasn't been used for years.

I came across it completely by accident. There were roadworks on the route I normally take, so I ended up cutting through an industrial estate and coming out onto the water. I remember thinking it was odd that I'd lived here for six years and never known it was there. That was two summers ago, and I've been going most weeks ever since.

What I do is fairly unvarying. I walk for about twenty minutes, as far as a set of lock gates, and then I sit on the beam of the gate with my feet over the water. Sometimes I take a coffee, though half the time I forget. The important thing, I think, is that there's no phone signal down there at all, so the decision about whether to look at my phone gets taken away from me.

As for why it helps — it isn't really the quiet on its own, because it isn't silent. There's water moving through the gates the whole time and a low hum from the ring road. It's more that nothing there is waiting for me. At home there's always something in my line of sight that needs doing, whereas on the towpath the only thing in front of me is water. I find I do the actual thinking on the walk back rather than while I'm sitting there, which suggests it's the walking that does half the work. Either way, it's the only twenty minutes in my week when nobody can reach me.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and a present perfect replace the band 6's run of flat past simples.
'Tucked away', 'came across', 'in my line of sight' — chunks doing the descriptive work.
'What I do is' and 'as for why' shape the turn; nothing is joined with a bare 'so'.

model_answers.transcript:
The place is a stretch of canal towpath behind a derelict mill, about a quarter of an hour on foot from where I live, and I stumbled on it entirely by chance.

There were roadworks on my usual route, so I cut through an industrial estate and came out on the water, and I can remember standing there faintly annoyed with myself — six years in the same postcode and I'd never once gone two streets further. Not that it's picturesque, particularly. It's a working waterway with rubbish in the reeds.

What I do there barely varies. Twenty minutes on foot to a set of lock gates, then I sit on the beam with my feet hanging over the water for as long as I can be bothered. There's no signal down there, which means the question of whether to check my phone simply never comes up, and that turns out to matter far more than the quiet does.

Because it isn't quiet, in fairness. Water comes through the gates the whole time and there's a drone from the ring road behind the trees. What it is, is undemanding — nothing on that towpath is waiting for me to deal with it, whereas at home there's never a sightline without a job in it. And I've noticed the thinking tends to happen on the walk back rather than on the gate itself, which makes me suspect that what I actually go for isn't the place at all. It's the twenty minutes of being unreachable.

model_answers.transcript:
I would like to describe a park which I use. It is near my house, about ten minutes if I walk, and I pass a church to arrive there.

It is not a big park. There is a football field, and there is a path around it, and there is some trees on one side. Also there is a small playground for the children.

I go there three times in a week, in the morning, because I like to run. I run three or four times around the path and then I go home. On Sunday I go with my niece and she plays in the playground. She is five years old and she loves the swings very much.

If they build on it, it will be very bad for me. Because I don't have another place to run near my house. And also for my niece it is not good, she has nowhere to play. Many people use this park, old people, young people, everybody. So I think it is very important and I hope they don't build on it. This is the green space that I use.

Three consecutive sentences begin 'there is', and the turn lists the contents.
'Big', 'small', 'very bad', 'very important' — the evaluation is all size and intensity.

model_answers.label: The target — same park, better language
model_answers.transcript:
It's a recreation ground about ten minutes from my front door, past the church and over a footbridge. Officially it has a name, but nobody uses it — everyone just calls it the rec.

It isn't much to look at. There's a football pitch that floods every winter, a tarmac path round the outside, and a line of lime trees along the road that take most of the traffic noise out. The far corner is completely overgrown, which I think is deliberate, because nobody has touched it in the four years I've been going.

I go three mornings a week, always before seven, and I do three laps of the path, which comes to about two miles. Then on Sundays I take my niece, and that's a different sort of visit altogether — my niece is at the age where the swings are the entire point of the outing, so we're there for an hour and I never make it round the path once.

As for what I'd miss if they built on it — it wouldn't really be the running, because I could run along the canal instead. It would be the fact that I see the same people every week without ever having arranged anything. There's a man with two greyhounds, a couple who always argue quietly by the gate, half a dozen people I only ever nod at. You can't get that indoors, and you certainly can't get it by planning it. That's what a scruffy field does that a nicer, further-away park couldn't.

what_lifts_it.point: A clean second conditional and two relative clauses where band 6 had 'there is' chains.
'The rec', 'scruffy', 'overgrown', 'floods every winter' — concrete instead of big and small.
The last bullet names what is lost and then argues why it can't be replaced.

annotations.span: It isn't much to look at.
annotations.label: Undersells before describing
annotations.why: Say the modest thing first; whatever follows then sounds honest.

annotations.span: a football pitch that floods every winter
annotations.label: Relative clause instead of a list
annotations.why: Attach a 'that' clause to one noun and the flat listing disappears.

annotations.span: if they built on it
annotations.label: Second conditional, correctly formed
annotations.why: Past tense in the if-clause, 'would' in the other half.

annotations.span: As for what I'd miss
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Announce this move and the fourth bullet stops getting squeezed into ten seconds.

annotations.span: I see the same people every week without ever having arranged anything
annotations.label: Names an abstract benefit precisely
annotations.why: Say what a place gives you, not that it is important to you.

annotations.span: half a dozen people I only ever nod at
annotations.label: Exact detail beats a general claim
annotations.why: One image like this replaces a whole sentence of adjectives.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place I use is a recreation ground ten minutes' walk away, over a footbridge and past a church. It has an official name on the sign, which I have never once heard anybody say out loud.

It's a fairly unpromising piece of land — a pitch that turns to mud by November, a tarmac loop round the edge, and a row of limes doing a surprising amount of work against the traffic. One corner has been left to go wild, and rather to my surprise the council seem to have done that on purpose. Whether by design or by neglect, it's the only patch with any birds in it.

My own use of it is dull and regular: three laps before seven, three mornings a week. Sundays are a different proposition, because I have my niece with me, and at four years old the swings are non-negotiable, so the running never happens at all. I've stopped pretending otherwise and started taking a flask.

What I'd miss, though, isn't the exercise. I could run somewhere else easily enough. It's that the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise — the man with the greyhounds, the couple who bicker by the gate, the handful of people I've nodded at for years without ever learning a name. Were it built on, that would simply stop, and it isn't the sort of thing you can reopen somewhere more convenient. Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Were it built on' — inversion replaces the band 7's standard second conditional.
'Unpromising', 'non-negotiable', 'bicker' are picked for shade rather than for size.
The close is an aphorism about places, not a summary of this place.

annotations.span: Were it built on, that would simply stop
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same conditional, higher register, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: the swings are non-negotiable
annotations.label: A formal word used playfully
annotations.why: Borrowing a work word for family life is a very natural move.

annotations.span: the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise
annotations.label: Abstracts the benefit in one phrase
annotations.why: Find the noun for what a place gives you and the answer lifts.

annotations.span: Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.
annotations.label: Closes on a general principle
annotations.why: End one rung above the story and the whole turn sounds considered.

annotations.span: a row of limes doing a surprising amount of work against the traffic
annotations.label: Long noun phrase in one run
annotations.why: Do not pause inside the phrase; keep it as a single group.

In the kitchen I do everything. I eat there, and also I work there in the morning with my laptop. I have a desk in my bedroom but I don't use it, I don't know why. When my friends come, we sit in the kitchen also.

Why I spend so much time there? Because it is sunny in the morning, and because it is comfortable. In the living room I feel I must relax, but in the kitchen I can do something and talk at the same time. It is more easy. So this is my favourite room and I spend there many hours every day.

what_caps_it.point: The turn is an inventory of the room, with no shape and a close that restates the card.

annotations.span: it was from the grandmother of my partner

model_answers.label: The target — same room, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The room I'd pick is the kitchen, which is at the back of the flat and is honestly the least impressive room we've got.

It's long and narrow, with units down one side and a table under the window at the far end. A galley kitchen, I think you'd call it. The table is far too big for the space — we inherited it from my partner's grandmother and nobody is willing to be the one who gets rid of it, so you have to turn sideways to get past. Out of the window there's a yard with three bins and a fig tree that has never produced a fig. It came with the flat and nobody has the heart to take it out.

I do more or less everything in there. I eat, obviously, but I also work at that table most mornings, even though there's a perfectly good desk in the bedroom that I've used about twice since we moved in. Friends end up in there too, because you can hand somebody a chair and carry on cooking at the same time.

Why it works is partly the light, since it faces east and it's the only room that gets any sun before midday. Mostly, though, it's that you can be doing something with your hands and talking at the same time, so nobody has to sit down opposite anybody. The living room always feels slightly formal, whereas nobody has ever been embarrassed to be standing in a kitchen. That's the real difference, I think.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect with 'since', a relative clause and a 'whereas' contrast replace flat statements.
'Galley', 'turn sideways to get past', 'slightly formal' — precision instead of size adjectives.
The fourth bullet tests the reason against another room instead of asserting it.

annotations.span: The room I'd pick is the kitchen

annotations.why: Decide before you start talking; hunting for a room on air always shows.

annotations.span: A galley kitchen, I think you'd call it.
annotations.label: Reaches for the technical word
annotations.why: Naming the type and flagging your uncertainty is a genuine band-7 move.

annotations.span: you have to turn sideways to get past
annotations.label: Shows the size, doesn't state it
annotations.why: One physical consequence is worth more than the word 'cramped'.

annotations.span: I do more or less everything in there.
annotations.label: Opens the bullet in one line
annotations.why: A short topic sentence hands you thirty seconds of obvious material.

annotations.span: there's a perfectly good desk in the bedroom that I've used about twice since we moved in
annotations.label: Present perfect with 'since'
annotations.why: Use 'since' plus the starting point whenever the situation still holds.

annotations.span: Why it works is partly the light
annotations.label: Names the explain bullet
annotations.why: Say 'why it works' aloud and the last bullet gets its full share of time.

annotations.span: whereas nobody has ever been embarrassed to be standing in a kitchen
annotations.label: Contrast plus present perfect
annotations.why: 'Whereas' joins two rooms and makes the comparison do real work.

annotations.span: it's the only room that gets any sun before midday
annotations.label: Stress falls on 'only'
annotations.why: The word carrying the contrast takes the beat; everything else stays level.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
It would have to be the kitchen, which is at the back of the flat and, objectively, the least attractive room in it. I've never once shown it to a visitor on purpose, and yet that is where they all end up.

It's a galley — units along one wall, a table at the far end under a window that looks onto a yard containing three bins and a fig tree which has stubbornly refused to fruit. The table itself is absurd for the space. It came down to us from my partner's grandmother, and since none of us is willing to be the one who disposes of it, we simply edge round it several times a day.

Practically everything happens in there. I eat, I work at that table most mornings, and I've barely touched the desk in the bedroom since the afternoon it was assembled. Even visitors drift in, which I've come to think is the point of the room: you can hand somebody a chair and carry on chopping, and nobody is required to perform. That was never planned; it simply turned out to be true.

What makes it work isn't really the light, though it does face east. It's that a kitchen gives you something to do with your hands while you talk. Sitting down opposite someone in a living room is a commitment; standing about in a kitchen isn't. Which is probably why the smartest room in most homes is also the emptiest one.

what_lifts_it.point: 'None of us is' and a fronted gerund subject go a step past band 7's relative clauses.
'Absurd', 'edge round', 'stubbornly refused' are chosen for shade, not for difficulty.
It closes on a claim about homes in general rather than about this kitchen.

annotations.span: since none of us is willing to be the one who disposes of it
annotations.label: Agreement after 'none of us'
annotations.why: 'None' takes a singular verb; the plural noun after it is a trap.

annotations.span: a fig tree which has stubbornly refused to fruit
annotations.label: A verb with a personality
annotations.why: Giving an object a human verb is precise and sounds completely natural.

annotations.span: we simply edge round it several times a day
annotations.label: The verb carries the size problem
annotations.why: Say what the space forces you to do and drop the adjective entirely.

annotations.span: Sitting down opposite someone in a living room is a commitment; standing about in a kitchen isn't.
annotations.label: Two balanced clauses, one idea
annotations.why: Parallel clauses land an abstract point without any linking words at all.

annotations.span: Which is probably why the smartest room in most homes is also the emptiest one.
annotations.label: Ends a rung above the story
annotations.why: Turn the last sentence into a claim about homes rather than yours.

I want to describe a place which is very crowded. It is the market in my city centre. It is an old building with glass roof, and inside there are many stalls, maybe forty.

It is crowded every Saturday, especially in the morning between ten and one o'clock. There is only one way to walk inside, so when the people stop to speak, nobody can pass. It is very difficult to move.

model_answers.label: The target — same market, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd choose is the covered market in the middle of town, which is an iron and glass hall from the 1880s with about forty stalls in it.

It's busy most days, but Saturday between about ten and one is when it becomes genuinely unpleasant. There's only one main aisle running the length of the building, so the whole thing behaves like a bottleneck — if two people stop to talk in the middle, everything behind them comes to a standstill. And they do stop, constantly, because half the town is in there at once. Nobody plans for that.

The reason so many go is partly price, since the fruit and veg is a fraction of what the supermarket charges, and partly loyalty, because the stalls have been run by the same families for years. My mother still refuses to buy fish anywhere else. She's been buying from the same man since before I was born, and she isn't alone in that.

How I feel about it depends entirely on what I'm there for. If I need something specific, I find it genuinely stressful — you can't move, you can't hear what anybody is saying, and it takes forty minutes to do fifteen minutes of shopping. But if I've got no particular plan, it's the only place in town where I run into people I haven't seen for months, and that only happens because it's crowded. So I've more or less stopped resenting it. I just go early when I'm in a hurry.

annotations.why: Keep the beat identical across the pair and let the second one fall.

annotations.label: Cost shown as a contrast

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'd pick the covered market in town — a Victorian hall with an iron roof, forty-odd stalls, and a single aisle running the entire length of it. It has looked more or less the same since the 1880s.

That one aisle is the whole problem. On a Saturday morning, roughly ten till one, the place is heaving, and since there's nowhere to step aside, two people greeting each other in the middle will bring the building to a halt. Which they do, endlessly, because half the town is in there at the same time.

What draws everybody is partly cost, as the fruit and veg goes for a fraction of supermarket prices, and partly loyalty, because most of the stalls have been in the same families for two or three generations and buying elsewhere feels faintly disloyal. My mother has used the same fishmonger for thirty years and would not dream of changing.

As for how I feel about it, that depends on what I've come for. Needing something specific, I find it close to unbearable — you shuffle, you can't hear, and a fifteen-minute errand swallows an hour. Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town where you run into people by accident rather than by arrangement. That isn't a small thing, and it exists precisely because the place is too full. So I've made my peace with it, and I do the real shopping at half past eight.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a place where I was going when I was a child. It was an old railway near the house of my grandparents. The train was not there any more, so it is only trees and bushes, and there was a hole in the fence, so we can go inside.

I went there with my brother and two boys from our street. We go there every day in the summer holiday, when I was seven, eight, until maybe twelve years old.

We did many things there. We took some wood from a building place and we make a house, but always it is falling down and we build it again. In August we eat the blackberries. Also we put coins on the rail because we wanted to make them flat.

I remember it very well because it was our place, only for children. No adults came there. So we can do everything we want. Now it is a bicycle road with a bench, and my nephew goes there, but he doesn't know about our house. It is a little bit sad, but it is normal. This is the place from my childhood.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative drops into the present six times, including inside the modals.
Every stage of the story arrives in the same flat two-clause sentence.
'Many things', 'very well', 'a little bit sad' — the wording never gets more exact.

annotations.span: I remember it very well because it was our place, only for children.
annotations.label: Answers the last bullet directly
annotations.why: Keep this — it gives a reason instead of describing more scenery.

annotations.span: I want to tell about a place
annotations.label: 'Tell' with nobody to tell
annotations.why: Say 'talk about' or 'tell you about'; 'tell' needs a person.

annotations.span: so it is only trees and bushes
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: 'It was just trees and bushes.' Set the tense and hold it.

annotations.span: we make a house, but always it is falling down and we build it again
annotations.label: Three tense slips in one line
annotations.why: 'We made a den, but it kept falling down and we rebuilt it.'

annotations.span: So we can do everything we want.
annotations.label: Modal left in the present
annotations.why: 'We could do whatever we wanted.' Past story, past modal.

annotations.span: This is the place from my childhood.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's wording
annotations.why: End on what the place gave you, not on the title of the task.

model_answers.label: The target — same memory, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd talk about is an old railway embankment at the end of the street where my grandparents lived. The line had closed long before I was born, so by the time we found it, it was completely wild — brambles, birch trees, and a fence with a gap in it that everybody's parents pretended not to know about.

I went up there with my brother and two boys from the next street, more or less every day of the summer holidays, from when I was about seven until I was twelve or thirteen and it suddenly stopped being interesting.

What we did there was mostly build things. We dragged pallets up from behind the builders' yard and made a den against the bank, which collapsed regularly and got rebuilt slightly better each time. We picked blackberries in August, and we spent an unreasonable amount of time trying to flatten coins on the one length of rail that was still there. None of it was allowed, strictly speaking, and none of it was ever stopped.

As for why it's stayed with me so clearly — I think it's because it was the first place that was properly ours. Nobody had planned it for us and no adult ever came up there, so whatever happened was entirely our own doing. It's a cycle path now, tarmacked and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den was. My nephew rides along it and has no idea. I'm glad it's used, but there's nothing about it now that a child could claim.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a passive hold the timeline that band 6 kept losing.
'Pretended not to know about', 'an unreasonable amount of time' — chunks with attitude in them.
The turn ends in the present day, which closes the story instead of stopping it.

annotations.span: The line had closed long before I was born
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the background
annotations.why: One backshift early on puts two layers of time into the story.

annotations.span: a fence with a gap in it that everybody's parents pretended not to know about
annotations.label: One clause carries the whole atmosphere
annotations.why: Say what the adults did rather than saying that you felt free.

annotations.span: What we did there was mostly build things.
annotations.label: Heads the bullet before filling it
annotations.why: Give the heading first and the examples come out without hesitation.

annotations.span: we spent an unreasonable amount of time
annotations.label: Understatement doing the evaluating
annotations.why: This chunk transfers to anything you did too much of.

annotations.span: As for why it's stayed with me so clearly
annotations.label: Signals the explain bullet
annotations.why: Announce it and the last thirty-five seconds go where they belong.

annotations.span: Nobody had planned it for us and no adult ever came up there
annotations.label: Two negatives, both in past forms
annotations.why: Negative past clauses handled cleanly are strong grammar evidence.

annotations.span: It's a cycle path now, tarmacked and signposted
annotations.label: Brings the story into the present
annotations.why: A then-and-now switch adds a tense and ends the turn naturally.

annotations.span: there's nothing about it now that a child could claim
annotations.label: Pitch falls on 'claim'
annotations.why: Drop the pitch on the final content word so the ending sounds finished.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a disused railway embankment at the end of my grandparents' road. The line had been lifted decades earlier, so what remained was a long green corridor running behind the houses, reached through a gap in the fence that every parent on that street knew about and none of them ever mentioned.

I was up there with my brother and a couple of boys from the next street on most days of the summer, from about seven until the year I turned thirteen and abruptly stopped going.

Chiefly, we built. Pallets were hauled up from the builders' yard behind the church, a den went against the bank, it fell down within a fortnight, and we rebuilt it marginally better each time. There were blackberries in August, and an absurd amount of effort spent flattening coins on the last surviving stretch of rail. None of that was permitted and none of it was ever prevented.

Why it has stayed with me is straightforward enough: it was the first territory that belonged to us. Nothing about it had been provided, which is precisely what made it valuable — no adult had ever set foot up there, so everything that happened was our own work and our own fault. It's a cycle path now, resurfaced and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den stood. My nephew uses it and hasn't the faintest idea. I'm pleased it's in use. I just doubt any child will ever call it theirs.

what_lifts_it.point: Two passives and a past perfect passive replace band 7's active past forms.
'Lifted', 'hauled', 'territory', 'resurfaced' are precise rather than decorative.
It concedes the modern use and then refuses it, in two short sentences.

annotations.span: The line had been lifted decades earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect passive
annotations.why: Two grammar points in one clause, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: Pallets were hauled up from the builders' yard behind the church
annotations.label: Passive keeps the focus on the work
annotations.why: Switch to the passive when who did it is obvious and dull.

annotations.span: a long green corridor running behind the houses
annotations.label: One image replaces three sentences
annotations.why: Find the noun that carries the shape of the place and use it early.

annotations.span: an absurd amount of effort spent flattening coins
annotations.label: The adjective does the judging
annotations.why: Let one word carry the verdict so you never say 'we enjoyed it'.

annotations.span: I'm pleased it's in use. I just doubt any child will ever call it theirs.
annotations.label: Concedes, then holds
annotations.why: Give the fair point first and the reservation sounds earned, not sour.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a town in the mountains where I went last year in November. It is about three hours by car from my parents house.

Before I go, I think it will be very beautiful. I saw many photos on internet, with sun and colourful houses and people sitting outside. So I expected the same thing.

But when I arrived, there was fog everywhere. For two days I cannot see the mountains, and the mountains are the reason to go there. Also two cafés were closed for the winter, and the museum was closed too. I was very disappointed and I thought it is a waste of money.

But after, it became better. Because everything was closed, all the people were in the same café, and I talked with an old lady for all the afternoon. She lived there all her life and she told me many things about the tourists in the town. It was very interesting, more interesting than the photos. So in the end I was happy, but also a little bit strange feeling, because I wanted a place like the photos. This is my experience.

what_caps_it.point: Nothing is backshifted: 'I think it will be' and 'I thought it is' inside one past story.
The reversal is flagged with 'but after' and then never developed into a point.
'Very beautiful', 'very disappointed', 'very interesting' stand in for any precision.

annotations.span: Because everything was closed, all the people were in the same café
annotations.label: Cause before result
annotations.why: Keep this — a 'because' clause at the front organises the whole sentence.

annotations.span: Before I go, I think it will be very beautiful.
annotations.label: The whole sentence is present
annotations.why: 'Before I went, I'd thought it would be beautiful.' Backshift every verb.

annotations.span: For two days I cannot see the mountains
annotations.label: Present modal in a past story
annotations.why: 'I couldn't see the mountains.' Past story, past modal.

annotations.span: I thought it is a waste of money
annotations.label: No backshift after 'thought'
annotations.why: 'I thought it was a waste of money.' The reported clause moves back too.

annotations.span: for all the afternoon
annotations.label: An article that shouldn't be there
annotations.why: 'All afternoon' or 'the whole afternoon' — you cannot have both.

annotations.span: a little bit strange feeling
annotations.label: The feeling is never named
annotations.why: 'It left me slightly uncomfortable' actually answers the fourth bullet.

model_answers.label: The target — same trip, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a small town in the mountains, about three hours' drive from where my family live, and I went there for a long weekend in November.

What I'd expected was essentially the photographs. Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September — clear light, painted houses, people eating outside — so I'd built up quite a specific picture of wandering around in the sun and taking a great many photographs of my own.

What I actually got was fog. The whole valley was under cloud for two days and you couldn't see the mountains at all, which are the only reason anyone goes. Two of the three cafés had shut for the winter, the museum was closed for repairs, and the one bus up to the ridge wasn't running either. By the second morning I'd more or less decided the trip was a write-off.

And then it wasn't, oddly. Because everything else was shut, everyone still in the town ended up in the same café, and I spent an entire afternoon talking to a woman in her eighties who had lived there her whole life and had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place. I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day, and she wasn't remotely sentimental about any of it. So what I came away with was a slightly uncomfortable feeling — that the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me.

what_lifts_it.point: Four past perfects hold the expectation apart from the reality throughout.
'A write-off', 'built up a picture', 'a great deal to say' — chunks instead of intensifiers.
Two clearly marked turns, and the answer ends on a judgement about itself.

annotations.span: What I'd expected was essentially the photographs.
annotations.label: Answers bullet two in one line
annotations.why: State the expectation as a thing, then spend your time on the evidence.

annotations.span: Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a past clause
annotations.why: Backshift once and both layers of time stay obvious to the listener.

annotations.span: the trip was a write-off
annotations.label: One noun makes the judgement
annotations.why: Reuse 'a write-off' for any plan or day that came to nothing.

annotations.span: What I actually got was fog.
annotations.label: A short sentence marks the turn
annotations.why: Five words after a long sentence signal the reversal without a linker.

annotations.span: And then it wasn't, oddly.
annotations.label: A second, deliberate reversal
annotations.why: Two turns keep a listener with you far better than one does.

annotations.span: I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day
annotations.label: Comparative against a hypothetical
annotations.why: Comparing what happened with what didn't earns real grammar credit.

annotations.span: had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place
annotations.label: Reports an opinion without quoting
annotations.why: Summarising what somebody said avoids a long run of direct speech.

annotations.span: the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me
annotations.label: Contrastive stress on 'produced'
annotations.why: The entire point sits on one word, so give that word the beat.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This was a small mountain town three hours from my parents', and I went up for a long weekend at the end of November, which was my first mistake.

Everything I'd seen of the place had been photographed in September, mostly by people who had gone at the right time of year. Clear light, painted shutters, people eating outside — so that was the weekend I'd packed for and, in effect, paid for.

What I found was cloud. The valley stayed under it for two solid days, so the mountains, which are the entire point, might as well not have existed. Two of the three cafés had closed for the season, the museum was mid-refurbishment, and the bus up to the ridge had stopped running in October. By Saturday lunchtime I'd written the trip off completely.

Which is when it got interesting. With nothing else open, everybody still in the town converged on the one café that was, and I spent most of an afternoon with a woman in her eighties who'd been born in the next street and had a good deal to say — not much of it warm — about what tourism had done to the valley and to the people who had stayed in it. I came away having learned more than any amount of scenery would have taught me, and faintly uneasy with myself, because what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Might as well not have existed' and a cleft with a past perfect passive go past band 7.
'Converged', 'mid-refurbishment', 'not much of it warm' are dry and exact, never showy.
The self-criticism at the end is the point of the turn and it is made only once.

annotations.span: which was my first mistake
annotations.label: An aside that flags the structure
annotations.why: Signalling trouble early makes a listener wait for the payoff.

annotations.span: might as well not have existed
annotations.label: Modal perfect in a relative clause
annotations.why: A compact way of saying the whole thing failed, and it sounds spoken.

annotations.span: Which is when it got interesting.
annotations.label: Turns the story in five words
annotations.why: A short fragment after a long paragraph is the cleanest reversal available.

annotations.span: not much of it warm
annotations.label: Four words replace a sentence
annotations.why: An aside like this shows judgement without any adjective of your own.

annotations.span: what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect passive
annotations.why: Front the 'what' clause so the turn ends on the phrase that matters.
